one_liner: Proves the generalized semi-Clifford conjecture through Clifford hierarchy level 4 for prime-dimensional qudits.
why_it_matters: Clarifying level-4 Clifford hierarchy structure helps classify gates relevant to teleportation-based and fault-tolerant quantum computation.
detailed_summary: The work extends fixed-point methods for conjugation actions associated with Clifford hierarchy gates. By analyzing groups Gamma_1(U), Gamma_2(U), and related structures for U in C_k, it proves the generalized semi-Clifford conjecture for k <= 4 in any prime dimension d. It also identifies a sufficient group-theoretic condition expected to help study higher hierarchy levels.
main_result: Every Clifford-hierarchy gate up to level 4 in prime dimension is shown to be generalized semi-Clifford.
application_angle: The result sharpens the mathematical toolkit for fault-tolerant gate synthesis, gate teleportation, and qudit quantum information protocols.

title: Rayleigh-Wood Threshold Controls Nonlinear Photon Correlations in Atomic Arrays
abstract: Two-dimensional atomic arrays provide versatile free-space quantum optical interfaces by coupling photons to collective lattice modes. Here we show that the Rayleigh--Wood anomaly provides a sharp control mechanism for both linear and nonlinear photon scattering from a single atomic layer. As the lattice spacing crosses the diffraction threshold, newly opened radiative channels rapidly broaden the dominant collective modes, converting specular reflection into diffuse off-axis scattering. In transmission, momentum-space Fano interference between the incident and collectively scattered fields produces single-photon intensity zeros that strongly reshape the momentum-space correlation pattern. An integrated nonlinear contrast reveals a pronounced channel asymmetry: upon opening the Rayleigh channels, the connected two-photon contribution drops by several orders of magnitude relative to the factorized background in transmission, while remaining close to unity in reflection. These results establish radiative diffraction thresholds as a control principle for quantum nonlinear optics in single-layer atomic arrays.
one_liner: Shows Rayleigh-Wood diffraction thresholds sharply tune linear and nonlinear photon correlations in 2D atomic arrays.
why_it_matters: It identifies lattice diffraction thresholds as a control knob for free-space quantum nonlinear optics at the single-layer level.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes photon scattering from a two-dimensional atomic layer as the lattice spacing crosses the Rayleigh-Wood diffraction threshold. Opening new radiative channels broadens dominant collective modes, redirects specular reflection into off-axis diffuse scattering, and creates transmission intensity zeros through momentum-space Fano interference. The connected two-photon contribution drops by orders of magnitude in transmission while remaining near unity in reflection.
main_result: Rayleigh-Wood thresholds are shown to control both scattering channels and nonlinear two-photon correlations in atomic arrays.
application_angle: This mechanism is useful for designing free-space quantum optical interfaces, nonlinear photon routing, and array-based quantum communication components.

title: Entangling Atomic Quantum Memories Using High-Order Modulated Coherent States
abstract: High-order coherent-state modulation and collective midpoint measurements enable multi-ebit entanglement distribution between cavity-coupled atomic memories. An SRM-inspired 16-QAM receiver achieves $1.75$ ebits per network mode use at $0.5$~dB end-to-end loss, exceeding single-qubit-per-mode benchmarks by $5.8$~dB and lying $3.8$~dB below the half-link capacity bound. The advantage persists for per-interface loss below $0.2$~dB and calibrated phase errors below $0.2π$. For 4-QAM, an optimized POVM with twice as many outcomes raises the achievable rate by $4.0\%$, revealing measurement-design headroom.
one_liner: High-order coherent-state modulation enables multi-ebit entanglement distribution between cavity-coupled atomic memories.
why_it_matters: It points to higher-rate quantum-repeater links by packing more entanglement per optical network mode under low-loss conditions.
detailed_summary: The work proposes using high-order modulated coherent states and collective midpoint measurements to entangle remote cavity-coupled atomic memories. A 16-QAM receiver inspired by square-root measurements reaches 1.75 ebits per network mode use at 0.5 dB end-to-end loss, outperforming single-qubit-per-mode benchmarks by 5.8 dB. The analysis also shows robustness thresholds for interface loss and phase error, plus a 4.0% rate gain from an optimized higher-outcome POVM for 4-QAM.
main_result: The protocol distributes up to 1.75 ebits per network mode use with 16-QAM coherent-state modulation at 0.5 dB loss.
application_angle: Higher-dimensional optical modulation could improve entanglement throughput in quantum networks and memory-based repeater architectures.

title: Relative entropy of entanglement and tripartite minimal surface
abstract: We propose a holographic dual of the relative entropy of entanglement for a boundary tripartition $A:B:C$. Our proposal is that, at the leading order, \begin{align} E_R(ρ_{AB}) = \frac{1}{4G_N}\Big[\mathrm{Area}(Γ_{\min}) - \mathrm{Area}(γ_{AB})\Big] \notag \end{align} where $Γ_{\min}$ is the minimal bulk tripartition surface and $γ_{AB}$ is the minimal surface homologous to $AB$. For a general random tensor network, we prove the corresponding upper bound by constructing a separable state associated with $Γ_{\min}$ and evaluating its relative entropy. We also establish the matching lower bound rigorously for networks of one, two, and three Haar random tensors by bounding the maximal tripartite product-state overlap. In appropriate geometries, the minimal tripartition surface can form a nontrivial tri-junction resembling the Mercedes logo. The proof proceeds by sequential optimization over candidate product states, which has a natural geometric interpretation as a local search for the minimal tripartition surface.
one_liner: A holographic proposal links relative entropy of entanglement to a tripartite minimal bulk surface.
why_it_matters: Although theoretical, it sharpens geometric tools for multipartite entanglement that may influence quantum-information models of many-body systems.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes a leading-order holographic dual for the relative entropy of entanglement in a boundary tripartition, expressed through the area difference between a minimal tripartition surface and the minimal surface homologous to AB. For random tensor networks, it proves an upper bound using an explicitly constructed separable state and establishes matching lower bounds for networks with one to three Haar random tensors. The construction admits nontrivial tri-junction geometries and frames the optimization as a geometric local search.
main_result: The authors derive and partially prove a tripartite minimal-surface formula for relative entropy of entanglement in random tensor network settings.
application_angle: The result is mainly foundational, but it may guide entanglement diagnostics for complex quantum states used in quantum simulation and photonic tensor-network models.

title: Experimental Demonstration of Chiral Bound States in the Continuum Enabled by Time-reversal Symmetry Breaking
abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) provide a powerful route to optical resonances with vanishing radiation loss and enhanced light-matter interactions. Of particular interest are chiral BICs, whose resonant states exhibit intrinsic circular polarization and spin-selective radiation. Magneto-optical photonic crystals have recently been predicted to host such states through time-reversal-symmetry breaking. Here, we experimentally demonstrate chiral BICs induced by time-reversal symmetry breaking in a magneto-optical photonic crystal, where an out-of-plane magnetic field lifts a degenerate BIC pair into two nondegenerate resonances with opposite circular polarizations. Numerical simulations reveal the associated chiral phase vortices and strong spin-selective radiation, while microwave measurements confirm the predicted behavior through angle-resolved transmission spectra and pronounced broadband circular dichroism. Our results establish an experimental platform for exploring chiral BIC physics in magneto-optical photonic structures, opening new opportunities for spin-selective photonics.
one_liner: Magneto-optical photonic crystals experimentally realize chiral bound states in the continuum under broken time-reversal symmetry.
why_it_matters: Chiral BICs offer low-loss, spin-selective resonances for compact nonreciprocal and polarization-selective photonic hardware.
detailed_summary: The study experimentally demonstrates chiral bound states in the continuum in a magneto-optical photonic crystal subjected to an out-of-plane magnetic field. The field lifts a degenerate BIC pair into two nondegenerate resonances with opposite circular polarizations. Numerical simulations identify chiral phase vortices and spin-selective radiation, while microwave angle-resolved transmission measurements show the expected resonance splitting and broadband circular dichroism.
main_result: An out-of-plane magnetic field creates experimentally observed chiral BIC resonances with opposite circular polarizations.
application_angle: The platform could support spin-selective filters, sensors, emitters, and nonreciprocal photonic components with enhanced light-matter interaction.

title: Classical Algorithms for Function Computation in Gaussian Boson Sampling
abstract: Gaussian boson sampling (GBS) seeks quantum advantage by sampling photon-number patterns generated with squeezed inputs and passive linear optics. Many proposed GBS applications instead target function computation by applying functions to mode-resolved photon-number outcomes---a natural form of experimental postprocessing that produces classical outputs. Sampling hardness alone, however, does not determine the complexity of these tasks. By analyzing the irreducible decomposition of fixed-photon-number operator spaces, we prove that the expectation value of every such function in the average case over passive linear-optical networks can be classically evaluated for inputs with finite squeezing strength. We also provide a classical algorithm that estimates this value to inverse-polynomial additive error. The result provides new theoretical tools for analyzing linear-optical quantum systems, helps clarify the origin of current GBS hardness evidence, and inspires new applications of GBS with genuine quantum advantages.
one_liner: The paper gives classical algorithms for average-case function computation over finite-squeezing Gaussian boson sampling outputs.
why_it_matters: It narrows where GBS applications can claim quantum advantage by separating sampling hardness from postprocessed function estimation.
detailed_summary: The authors analyze tasks where functions are applied to mode-resolved photon-number outcomes from Gaussian boson sampling experiments. Using irreducible decompositions of fixed-photon-number operator spaces, they prove that average-case expectation values of such functions can be classically evaluated for passive linear-optical networks with finite squeezing. They also provide an algorithm that estimates these values to inverse-polynomial additive error.
main_result: For finite squeezing, average-case expectations of arbitrary postprocessed GBS output functions admit efficient classical estimation to inverse-polynomial additive error.
application_angle: The result helps benchmark photonic quantum advantage claims and steers GBS application design toward tasks less vulnerable to classical postprocessing algorithms.

title: Semi-Quantum Cryptography with Certified Deletion
abstract: Certified deletion allows a client to upload encrypted data to a server as a quantum state, then later request that the server delete their data and detect whether the server complies. If verification passes, then the data on the server will remain hidden even if the decryption key is later leaked. In publicly verifiable certified deletion, the verification key is published so that anyone may check for deletion compliance. In this work, we give a general compiler to publicly verifiable certified deletion that allows the client to initially upload the *quantum* ciphertext using purely *classical* communication, assuming the post-quantum hardness of LWE in the plain model. Our approach can be applied to a wide variety of primitives, including commitments and public-key, attribute-based, identity-based, and fully-homomorphic encryption. Moreover, our constructions allow the client to classically manage the encrypted data beyond just verifying its deletion. The classical client may non-destructively audit the ciphertext via a Proof of No Intrusion to check whether it has been leaked to a third party. The classical client may also retrieve the data while simultaneously verifying its deletion from the server. Thus, they do not have to choose between retrieving the data and protecting it against future key leakage. As our core technical contribution, we give a classical-communication protocol and simulation technique that allows adapting purification-based security arguments for BB84-style states which are prepared through classical interaction. It makes the required purification available in a hybrid experiment, despite the classical transcript uniquely determining the prepared state in a real execution.
one_liner: A compiler enables publicly verifiable certified deletion with a classical client and quantum ciphertext upload.
why_it_matters: It reduces quantum requirements on clients while preserving deletion guarantees against later key leakage under post-quantum assumptions.
detailed_summary: The paper constructs a compiler for publicly verifiable certified deletion where the client communicates classically while the server receives a quantum ciphertext. Assuming LWE hardness, the approach applies to commitments and several encryption types, including public-key, attribute-based, identity-based, and fully homomorphic encryption. It also supports non-destructive audits through Proof of No Intrusion and data retrieval with simultaneous deletion verification.
main_result: The work shows how to realize certified deletion and ciphertext auditing through classical client interaction with post-quantum security assumptions.
application_angle: This could make quantum-secure cloud storage and deletion compliance more deployable by removing the need for clients to transmit quantum states directly.

title: Tight Post-Quantum Parallel Repetition for Private-Coin Arguments
abstract: We show that assuming the existence of homomorphic encryption, parallel repetition of all interactive arguments (after being run under homomorphic encryption) reduces the soundness error at a tight exponential rate even in the post-quantum setting. Moreover, we generalize this result to hold for threshold verifiers, where the parallel repeated verifier accepts if and only if at least $t$ of the executions are accepted (for some threshold $t$). Prior to this work, these results were known only when the cheating prover was assumed to be classical, and it was not known how to achieve tight bounds. As a corollary, we construct the first constant-round succinct argument for $\mathsf{QMA}$ with negligible completeness and soundness errors assuming only the existence of quantum homomorphic encryption.
one_liner: The paper proves tight post-quantum parallel repetition for private-coin arguments run under homomorphic encryption.
why_it_matters: It strengthens cryptographic proof systems against quantum adversaries and yields succinct arguments for QMA under quantum homomorphic encryption.
detailed_summary: The work proves that parallel repetition of interactive arguments, after execution under homomorphic encryption, reduces soundness error at a tight exponential rate even against quantum cheating provers. The theorem also extends to threshold verifiers that accept when at least a chosen number of repetitions accept. As a corollary, it constructs constant-round succinct arguments for QMA with negligible completeness and soundness errors from quantum homomorphic encryption.
main_result: Parallel repetition achieves tight exponential soundness amplification for encrypted private-coin arguments in the post-quantum setting.
application_angle: The result supports more efficient quantum-safe verification protocols, including succinct verification of quantum computations and cryptographic primitives.

title: Constant Rate Codes with Fully Addressable Transversal T: Good Codes, Sparse Checks
abstract: Recent work by Wills constructed codes with constant rate and transversal $T$. Extending this line of work, we construct asymptotically good CSS codes with \textbf{fully addressable} transversal $T$, permitting selective control over which logical qubits receive a $T$ gate. We also give Pauli-LDPC codes with transversal $T$ and growing distance at vanishing rate; and a protected-subsystem construction with fully addressable transversal $T$, constant protected rate, distance $Ω(\sqrt n)$, and sparse (non-Pauli) checks. More generally, we obtain asymptotically good binary codes with full transversal addressability for every fixed finite-order one-qubit gate, retaining CSS realizations for dyadic phase gates such as $\sqrt T$ and using generally nonadditive codes for rotations such as $R_z(π/7)$. The remaining challenge is to construct asymptotically good Pauli-LDPC codes with fully addressable transversal non-Clifford one-qubit gates.
one_liner: Constructs good CSS and related codes with fully addressable transversal non-Clifford gates, including selective logical T operations.
why_it_matters: Selective transversal non-Clifford gates could reduce routing and magic-state overheads in fault-tolerant quantum processors.
detailed_summary: The work extends constant-rate transversal-T code constructions to fully addressable logical gates, so chosen logical qubits can receive T while others do not. It also gives Pauli-LDPC variants with growing distance at vanishing rate and a protected-subsystem construction with sparse non-Pauli checks. The broader framework covers fixed finite-order one-qubit gates, with CSS realizations for dyadic phase gates and nonadditive codes for other rotations.
main_result: The paper demonstrates asymptotically good binary and CSS code families with full transversal addressability for several finite-order logical gates.
application_angle: This targets lower-overhead logical gate execution in scalable quantum computing architectures.

title: Entropy threshold: A simple proxy for performance of quantum error correction
abstract: The rapidly growing landscape of quantum error-correction (QEC) protocols has produced a wealth of numerical data, but comparatively few heuristics for understanding and predicting their performance. Here, we develop a simple entropy-based proxy that predicts the thresholds of a variety of QEC protocols, ranging from the code-capacity setting of Clifford-deformed surface codes with biased Pauli or erasure noise to the circuit-level noise model of the surface or color codes with flag qubits. Our proxy estimates the threshold by locally comparing the noise entropy with the error information gained via stabilizer measurements (or spacetime detectors and flag outcomes in the circuit-level settings). Despite neglecting correlations between stabilizer outcomes and the contribution from code degeneracy, the proxy captures the main trends across diverse settings and yields threshold estimates in good agreement with numerical results. Our work develops much-needed phenomenology that enables simple back-of-the-envelope estimates of QEC performance, recovering and providing an explanation for the results of computationally intensive detailed simulations.
one_liner: Introduces an entropy-based proxy that estimates QEC thresholds across code-capacity and circuit-level settings.
why_it_matters: Fast threshold estimates can guide hardware and code choices before committing to expensive large-scale QEC simulations.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes estimating QEC thresholds by locally comparing noise entropy with information extracted from stabilizer measurements, spacetime detectors, and flag outcomes. Despite ignoring some syndrome correlations and degeneracy effects, the proxy tracks numerical threshold trends across deformed surface codes, surface codes, and color codes. It functions as a phenomenological back-of-the-envelope model for diverse noise assumptions.
main_result: The main result is a simple entropy-threshold proxy that agrees well with detailed numerical threshold data over multiple QEC settings.
application_angle: It can speed early-stage design of fault-tolerant hardware by ranking codes and noise regimes with minimal computation.

title: Provable Classical and Quantum Local Algorithms for Max-$k$-Cut and Quantum Advantage at Moderate Girth
abstract: Broadening the study of quantum optimization algorithms from binary to $k$-element alphabets has been shown to open new avenues for potential quantum advantage. A quantum advantage claim for approximate optimization requires showing that, under the same assumptions, an efficient quantum algorithm provably achieves a better performance than can be proven for the best known efficient classical algorithms. We study local classical and quantum algorithms for Max-$k$-Cut on $d$-regular graphs of girth $g$. We advance classical algorithms for this problem by developing a local vector algorithm based on the explicit vector construction of Thompson, Parekh, and Marwaha (TPM). Our algorithm gives the best provable cut fraction guarantee among known efficient classical algorithms on regular graphs for $k\geq3$. To evaluate the performance of QAOA under identical assumptions of girth and regularity, we develop tensor network techniques for general $d$ and $k \geq 2$. In addition, using an equivalence to a coupled qudit--boson system, we compute the QAOA performance in the infinite-degree limit. Together, these techniques give provable guarantees on QAOA performance on large graphs. Despite the improvements we introduce to the classical algorithm, QAOA achieves a better cut fraction guarantee for depths $p\geq 9$, corresponding to girth $g\geq 20$, for both finite- and infinite-degree regimes. Thus, we obtain an apparent quantum advantage from applying QAOA to the Max-$k$-Cut problem.
one_liner: Compares improved classical local algorithms with QAOA for Max-k-Cut and finds provable QAOA advantage at moderate graph girth.
why_it_matters: Provable optimization advantages clarify where near-term quantum algorithms may outperform matched classical baselines.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a stronger classical local vector algorithm for Max-k-Cut on d-regular graphs using the TPM construction. It then analyzes QAOA under the same girth and regularity assumptions using tensor-network methods and an infinite-degree mapping to a coupled qudit-boson system. For depths p at least 9, corresponding to girth at least 20, QAOA achieves a better provable cut fraction than the improved classical guarantee.
platform_or_system: QAOA on regular graph optimization instances
main_result: The work reports a provable QAOA performance advantage for Max-k-Cut at depth p>=9 under matched graph assumptions.
application_angle: It strengthens the case for quantum processors as useful accelerators for structured combinatorial optimization.

title: Quantum circuit compilation with constant overhead
abstract: Compiling a continuous gate set to a discrete universal gate set generally incurs an overhead. A circuit composed of $G$ arbitrary one- and two-qubit gates can be $ε$-approximated by a sequence of gates from $\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}$ by replacing each original gate by a sequence of $O(\log(G/ε))$ elementary gates. We show that this overhead can be avoided using adaptivity for polynomial-sized circuits with inverse-polynomial target error, which is optimal.
one_liner: Shows adaptive compilation can approximate polynomial-size quantum circuits over H,T,CNOT with constant overhead.
why_it_matters: Constant-overhead compilation would directly reduce logical depth and resource costs in fault-tolerant quantum computers.
detailed_summary: Standard discrete-gate compilation replaces each arbitrary one- or two-qubit gate with a sequence scaling as O(log(G/epsilon)). This paper shows that, for polynomial-sized circuits and inverse-polynomial target error, adaptivity can avoid that scaling and achieve constant overhead. The result addresses an optimal compilation regime for universal fault-tolerant gate sets.
main_result: The main demonstrated capability is constant-overhead approximation of polynomial-size circuits using the discrete H,T,CNOT gate set with adaptivity.
application_angle: This could materially lower the compiled circuit cost for practical fault-tolerant workloads.

title: Metachecks in Bivariate Bicycle Codes: Syndrome Distance, Measurement Faults, and Repair Limits
abstract: Faulty syndrome measurements can corrupt an otherwise correct quantum-error correction step. Bivariate bicycle (BB) codes contain dependent stabilizer checks, so every valid syndrome obeys additional parity constraints, or metachecks. We study how far this built-in redundancy can identify measurement faults and when the remaining ambiguity is unavoidable, while separately checking the code's logical structure. A logical decomposition is used as a preliminary safety check: it identifies a $k/2$-dimensional annihilator subspace and a $k/2$-dimensional colon quotient, and the minimum-weight logical need not be visible from the annihilator side alone. On the measurement side, translation symmetry partitions syndrome locations into classes that carry identical metacheck information. This gives an exact characterization of the leading single-fault ambiguity, a bound on how many fault locations can be distinguished, and a family-level repair limit when the encoded dimension stays bounded while the block length grows. Under a static-data assumption, the same calculation gives the minimum number of checks that must be remeasured to remove every single-fault ambiguity. Exact finite-code calculations illustrate both regimes: all single measurement faults are distinguishable in a 72-qubit BB code, whereas the 144-qubit Gross code merges its 72 syndrome locations into 36 indistinguishable pairs. In a 108-qubit example, one logical component first appears at weight 12 while the other contains a weight-10 logical. Sustained phenomenological experiments show that joint data--measurement decoding is more robust than a separated repair stage on the more ambiguous codes. The resulting tests apply to general two-block BB codes, including non-coprime periods and repeated-root cases.
one_liner: Analyzes metachecks in bivariate bicycle codes to quantify measurement-fault ambiguity and repair limits.
why_it_matters: BB codes are hardware-relevant QEC candidates, and measurement-fault handling is crucial for realistic decoding performance.
detailed_summary: The paper studies dependent stabilizer checks in bivariate bicycle codes as metachecks that constrain valid syndromes and expose measurement faults. It characterizes when single measurement faults are distinguishable, including examples where a 72-qubit BB code resolves all single faults while the 144-qubit Gross code merges syndrome locations into ambiguous pairs. It also separates logical-structure checks from measurement-fault repair and finds joint data-measurement decoding more robust than a separated repair stage in ambiguous cases.
main_result: The work gives exact finite-code and family-level criteria for syndrome-fault distinguishability and remeasurement requirements in BB codes.
application_angle: These diagnostics inform decoder and measurement-schedule design for quantum LDPC hardware implementations.

title: Quantum Frozen--Oseen homotopy analysis method with LCHS for solving nonlinear partial differential equations
abstract: Nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) underpin computational fluid dynamics, yet resolving nonlinear transport on fine grids remains computationally demanding. Quantum linear-evolution algorithms offer a possible route to large-scale simulation but cannot directly propagate nonlinear coupling. Here we develop a Frozen--Oseen quantum homotopy method (FOQHAM) framework that links transport-aware auxiliary-operator selection to the size of the resulting linear representation. We freeze the full Fréchet derivative at a prescribed flow profile, retaining transport and profile-gradient coupling and close each prescribed finite-order homotopy hierarchy as a fixed affine linear system by product lifting. We formulate its propagation through Linear Combinations of Hamiltonian Simulations (LCHS), without outer homotopy iterations or profile updates. For spatially semidiscrete equations, we establish local approximation bounds and exact closure of the finite-order hierarchy. Classical tests on Burgers, Korteweg--de Vries, Zakharov--Kuznetsov, and one- and two-dimensional isothermal compressible Navier--Stokes equations provide numerical evidence of accurate non-iterative approximations in the tested regimes. The framework thus connects nonlinear PDE approximation to quantum linear evolution and offers a conditional path toward quantum acceleration.
one_liner: Formulates a Frozen-Oseen quantum homotopy method using LCHS to map nonlinear PDE approximations to linear quantum evolution.
why_it_matters: Efficient nonlinear PDE solvers are a major application target for quantum algorithms, especially in fluid and transport simulation.
detailed_summary: The paper freezes the full Frechet derivative at a prescribed flow profile, retaining transport and profile-gradient coupling while closing finite-order homotopy hierarchies as affine linear systems. It propagates the resulting representation using Linear Combinations of Hamiltonian Simulations without outer homotopy iterations or profile updates. Classical tests on Burgers, KdV, Zakharov-Kuznetsov, and compressible Navier-Stokes equations support accurate non-iterative approximations in tested regimes.
platform_or_system: quantum linear-evolution algorithms for nonlinear PDEs
main_result: The main result is a conditional framework that converts finite-order nonlinear PDE homotopy approximations into LCHS-compatible linear evolution problems.
application_angle: It sketches a route toward quantum acceleration for computational fluid dynamics and nonlinear transport modeling.

title: Breaking the Bounded Entanglement Barrier for Quantum Position Verification
abstract: Position verification, introduced by Chandran et al. (SIAM J. Computing 2014), allows verifiers to test a prover's claimed position by an interactive protocol. Classical position verification is impossible. Even for Quantum Position Verification (QPV), there always exists an LOCC (Local Operations and Classical Communication) attack if the adversary can hold an exponentially large amount of preshared entanglement. Somewhat surprisingly, we show that we can circumvent this barrier in the idealized continuous-time model, where time is represented by a real-valued parameter and challenge messages can be sent at a time sampled uniformly from a real interval. In this model, we give a BB84-based protocol that remains secure against any finite coalition of LOCC adversaries with arbitrary finite (possibly exponential) quantum storage and entanglement. Our construction can also be instantiated in the discrete-time model. Even though the previous impossibility results apply, we are able to obtain an information-theoretic QPV protocol in which the honest parties' total resources (communication and storage) can be significantly smaller than the adversarial resource bound. In fact, we can achieve any desired polynomial gap between honest parties and adversarial resources. To our knowledge, all previous protocols in the literature required resources of the honest parties to be at least as large as the adversarial entanglement. Interestingly, the resource gap between the honest and adversarial party resources in our protocol depends on how precisely time can be measured. As the precision of the best-known clock improves with further research, the resource gap in our protocol keeps increasing. In particular, the adversarial resource bound keeps increasing while the honest parties' resources remain largely the same. We call this the "I sleep, you work" paradigm.
one_liner: A timing-randomized BB84-style protocol gives QPV security against finite LOCC coalitions with arbitrary finite entanglement.
why_it_matters: It reopens information-theoretic quantum position verification by making adversarial entanglement cost scale with clock precision rather than honest resources.
detailed_summary: The paper studies quantum position verification in continuous time, where challenge emission times are sampled from a real interval. A BB84-based construction is shown secure against any finite coalition of LOCC adversaries with finite quantum storage and preshared entanglement. A discrete-time version still allows a polynomial resource gap between honest verifiers/prover and adversaries, with the gap tied to timing precision.
main_result: The main result is an information-theoretic QPV protocol whose honest resource use can be polynomially smaller than the adversarial entanglement/storage bound.
application_angle: This is relevant to location authentication and relativistic cryptographic primitives where security depends on timing and quantum communication constraints.

title: Optimal learning of covariant quantum states and channels
abstract: We give collective tomography protocols for quantum states and channels with known symmetries, using random purification and dilation to reduce learning to pure-state estimation. For states commuting with a compact-group representation with multiplicities $m_λ$, the optimal copy complexity is $Θ((\sum_λm_λ^2+\logη^{-1})/\varepsilon^2)$ for sufficiently small trace-distance error $\varepsilon$ and failure probability $η$ for the nontrivial case $\sum_λm_λ^2>1$. For $G$-covariant channels with finite-dimensional unitary representations of a compact group $G$, parallel $\widetilde{O}(D_G/\varepsilon^2)$ queries achieve a diamond-distance error $\varepsilon $ at fixed success probability $2/3$, where $D_G$ counts the real parameters of covariant Choi operators before imposing trace preservation. For permutation-covariant channels on $k$ qudits of fixed local dimension $d$, at sufficiently small fixed error and fixed success probability $2/3$, we obtain the optimal query scalings $Θ_d(k^{d^4-1})$ for diamond distance and $Θ_d(k^{d^4-d^2})$ for Choi trace distance. Furthermore, we resolve an open problem in quantum tomography of constructing efficient quantum circuits that approximate the Hayashi measurement for optimal pure-state estimation. We encode states in the symmetric subspace into bosonic occupation modes, realize the measurement by heterodyne detection and normalization, and approximate this procedure on qubits using the quantum Hermite transform. Combined with our symmetry-compatible purification and dilation circuits, this yields query-optimal and gate-efficient learners of permutation-covariant states and channels with gate complexity $O_d(\mathrm{poly}(k,\varepsilon^{-1},\logη^{-1}))$.
one_liner: Symmetry-aware collective tomography achieves optimal learning rates for covariant states and channels with efficient measurement circuits.
why_it_matters: It turns known physical symmetries into concrete savings for quantum device characterization and channel learning.
detailed_summary: The work gives collective tomography protocols for states and channels constrained by compact-group covariance, reducing learning to pure-state estimation via purification and dilation. It derives optimal copy/query scalings, including permutation-covariant channel scaling laws for k qudits at fixed local dimension. It also constructs efficient circuits approximating the Hayashi measurement using bosonic occupation encodings, heterodyne-style normalization, and the quantum Hermite transform.
main_result: The main result is query-optimal and gate-efficient tomography for covariant states and channels with provable trace- and diamond-distance guarantees.
application_angle: The methods can reduce characterization cost for photonic, atomic, or processor channels whose dynamics obey known symmetries.

title: Information Potential: A Variational Approach to Quantum Information Complexity
abstract: Quantum information complexity (QIC), introduced by Touchette [Touchette, STOC 2015], has been shown to be one of the most powerful methods for proving quantum communication complexity and has also been shown to be equal to amortized quantum communication complexity. Unfortunately, QIC is generally hard to analyze because it is a sum of quantum conditional mutual information terms, which are difficult to estimate. In this work, we introduce a new variational approach, the information potential, for analyzing QIC and proving quantum communication lower bounds inspired by the resolvent representation for quantum relative entropy. This approach connects the QIC of individual messages to a quadratic form, making it more amenable and thus enables us to bound the cumulative positive increments of the potential throughout an interactive quantum protocol by its QIC. Lower bounds on the growth of the potential therefore translate into lower bounds on both QIC and quantum communication complexity. As an application, we give an optimal $Ω(1/r)$ lower bound on the QIC of the two-bit $\mathsf{AND}$ function as well as an optimal $Ω(n/r)$ lower bound on the quantum communication complexity of $r$-round Set-Disjointness, answering an open problem in~[Braverman, Garg, Ko, Mao, Touchette FOCS 2015]. Moreover, we further prove a direct-sum theorem for bounded-round quantum communication complexity of Set Disjointness. With the tight bound on the QIC of $\mathsf{AND}$ function, we further establish a nearly tight tradeoff for the asymmetric quantum communication complexity of $\mathsf{Set} \mathsf{Disjointness}$: $(q_A+1)(q_B+1)=Ω(n)$, where $q_A$ and $q_B$ denote the total numbers of qubits sent by Alice and Bob, respectively.
one_liner: A variational information potential makes quantum information complexity lower bounds easier to prove for interactive protocols.
why_it_matters: Sharper communication lower bounds clarify when quantum protocols cannot efficiently solve distributed tasks, informing QComm limits.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces an information potential based on a variational, quadratic-form view of quantum information complexity. Growth of this potential across messages yields lower bounds on QIC and therefore on amortized quantum communication. The framework proves optimal bounds for two-bit AND and r-round Set Disjointness, plus a bounded-round direct-sum theorem and asymmetric tradeoff.
main_result: The main result is an optimal Omega(n/r) quantum communication lower bound for r-round Set Disjointness using the information-potential method.
application_angle: These limits help benchmark quantum networking and distributed-computing protocols against provable communication bottlenecks.

title: Constant-Overhead Injection into Quantum Codes
abstract: We construct the first known fault-tolerant scheme for injecting states into quantum error-correcting codes with constant space and time overhead. That is, we construct a family of constant-rate quantum error-correcting codes for which a set of bare physical qubits can be injected, i.e. fault-tolerantly encoded, into a code block. Similarly, a code state can be ejected, i.e. fault-tolerantly decoded, back into bare physical qubits. We show that these injection and ejection procedures succeed under circuit-level locally stochastic noise, while incurring just a small constant probability of corrupting each qubit, which is unavoidable for bare physical qubits. We also show how to perform fault-tolerant error correction and code-state preparation under locally stochastic noise. All of our gadgets can be implemented with constant quantum circuit depth (i.e. are single-shot), and with a number of physical qubits growing linearly with the number of logical qubits, assuming the ability to run polynomial-sized noiseless classical circuits on the side. We construct our quantum codes by taking a high-dimensional hypergraph product of classical LDPC codes, which in turn are a simplified version of Spielman's linear-time encodable codes (STOC'95). As our resulting product codes are only resilient to physical errors occurring with non-uniform probabilities across qubits, we then show how to concatenate with inner codes of various sizes to obtain fault-tolerance against uniform noise.
one_liner: A constant-rate code family supports single-shot fault-tolerant state injection and ejection with constant space-time overhead.
why_it_matters: State injection and decoding are core hardware operations, and constant overhead would ease scaling of fault-tolerant architectures.
detailed_summary: The paper constructs quantum LDPC-style codes from high-dimensional hypergraph products of simplified Spielman encodable classical codes. It gives constant-depth gadgets for injecting bare physical qubits into a code block and ejecting code states back to bare qubits under circuit-level locally stochastic noise. Concatenation with variable-size inner codes is used to obtain tolerance against uniform noise.
main_result: The main result is the first known constant space-and-time overhead scheme for fault-tolerant injection and ejection into quantum codes.
application_angle: This could simplify interfaces between physical qubits, encoded memory, and logical operations in scalable fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Reservoir- and Measurement-free Microwave Initialization of Semiconductor Spin Qubits
abstract: Scalable quantum processors require repeated qubit initialization throughout large arrays. In semiconductor spin qubits, fast initialization commonly relies on local reservoir access or measurement-based feedback, requiring dedicated infrastructure that becomes increasingly difficult to distribute as processors scale. Here, we demonstrate reservoir- and measurement-free initialization of a silicon spin-qubit pair in an industrially fabricated Si/SiGe quantum-dot device using a fixed sequence of microwave and baseband pulses. Odd spin-parity states relax to the singlet charge state, whereas blocked even spin-parity states are microwave-driven through the triplet manifold and subsequently converted to the singlet by singlet-triplet mixing and charge hybridization. Repeated cycles produce the singlet-associated charge outcome with a median probability of 99.4% across the sampled preparation states, while exchange spectroscopy independently verifies mapping to the target $|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle$ operational state. Microwave spectroscopy and time-domain measurements identify the dark-state-limited single-cycle transfer and the subsequent blockade-lifting dynamics that set the initialization time scale. The demonstrated pumping sequence uses approximately $12\,μ\mathrm{s}$ of microwave bursts and mixing dwells, while we project sub-microsecond initialization under improved device conditions. These results establish fixed-sequence microwave initialization as a scalable control primitive for semiconductor spin-qubit processors, based on singlet-triplet physics that can be adapted to platforms with suitable Pauli-blockade transitions.
one_liner: Fixed microwave and baseband pulse cycles initialize a Si/SiGe spin-qubit pair without reservoirs or measurement feedback.
why_it_matters: Removing local reservoirs and feedback infrastructure directly addresses a scaling bottleneck for semiconductor spin-qubit arrays.
detailed_summary: The experiment demonstrates reservoir- and measurement-free initialization in an industrially fabricated silicon Si/SiGe quantum-dot device. Odd-parity states relax to a singlet charge state, while blocked even-parity states are microwave-driven through triplet states and converted through singlet-triplet mixing and charge hybridization. Repeated cycles yield a median 99.4% singlet-associated charge outcome, with exchange spectroscopy confirming mapping to the target operational state.
main_result: The main result is 99.4% median preparation of the singlet-associated outcome using a fixed microwave/baseband pumping sequence.
application_angle: The approach offers a scalable initialization primitive for dense spin-qubit processors where reservoirs and local feedback are hard to distribute.

title: Parallel classical simulation of noisy shallow circuits: no quantum advantage in 1D
abstract: We consider quantum circuits consisting of $d$ layers of nearest-neighbor two-qubit gates acting on $n$ qubits arranged on a line, where every qubit is independently depolarized with a constant probability before each layer. We describe a randomized parallel algorithm which samples from the output distribution of any such circuit to within total variation error $δ$, with parallel runtime $2^{O(d)}\log\log(n/δ)$ and $n 2^{O(d)}$ elementary real-arithmetic operations. Without noise, the same approach gives an exact sampler with parallel runtime $O(\log n)$. For constant depth, we further show that the input/output behavior of the noisy quantum circuit is reproduced up to a constant error by a randomized $\mathsf{AC}^0$-circuit, that is, a Boolean circuit of polynomial size and constant depth with unbounded fan-in AND and OR gates and NOT gates. Consequently, every relation problem solved by a noisy constant-depth quantum circuit in one dimension is also solved, with essentially the same success probability, by a randomized $\mathsf{AC}^0$-circuit. This rules out, for noisy circuits in one dimension, the unconditional quantum advantage established for noisy shallow circuits in two and three dimensions, where polynomial-size classical circuits over the same gate set require depth $Ω(\log n/\log\log n)$. Our algorithm exploits the fact that depolarizing noise cuts a one-dimensional circuit into independent pieces of logarithmic width, each of which can be sampled exactly in parallel.
one_liner: A parallel sampler shows noisy constant-depth 1D nearest-neighbor circuits lack the shallow-circuit advantage seen in higher dimensions.
why_it_matters: It maps an important boundary of near-term quantum advantage by showing that 1D shallow noisy hardware is classically simulable.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes depth-d nearest-neighbor circuits on a 1D line with constant depolarizing noise before each layer. Noise breaks the circuit into independent logarithmic-width segments, enabling randomized parallel sampling within total variation error delta. For constant depth, the input-output behavior is reproduced to constant error by randomized AC0 circuits, contrasting with known noisy shallow-circuit advantage in 2D and 3D.
main_result: The main result is a randomized parallel classical sampler with runtime 2^{O(d)} log log(n/delta) and n 2^{O(d)} arithmetic operations.
application_angle: This helps focus experimental advantage efforts on geometries, noise regimes, or tasks where shallow quantum devices evade efficient classical simulation.

title: Excitation gap of a blockade structure with $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological order
abstract: Mathematically rigorous statements on the spectral gap of quantum many-body systems in the thermodynamic limit are notoriously difficult to prove -- yet they are of fundamental importance for classifying quantum phases of matter. Here we prove the existence of a finite excitation gap for a particular Hamiltonian which was proposed in [T. F. Maier et al., PRX Quantum 6, 030340 (2025)] and is motivated by the Rydberg platform. The Hamiltonian exhibits only two-body blockade interactions between two-level systems and has a topologically ordered ground state in the toric code phase. We show that our result also applies to a broader class of blockade Hamiltonians which realize non-Abelian quantum double phases and were proposed in [H. P. Büchler et al., Phys. Rev. B 114, 065113 (2026)]. The proof builds on known gap stability results and exploits the local symmetry of the studied models.
one_liner: Rigorous proof of a finite excitation gap for Rydberg-motivated blockade Hamiltonians with toric-code topological order.
why_it_matters: A proven gap strengthens the theoretical foundation for using blockade-based neutral-atom hardware to realize stable topological quantum memories.
detailed_summary: The paper proves a finite thermodynamic excitation gap for a two-body blockade Hamiltonian proposed for Rydberg platforms. The model has a toric-code-phase ground state, and the argument extends to broader blockade Hamiltonians designed to realize non-Abelian quantum double phases. The proof combines gap-stability machinery with local symmetry structure in the models.
main_result: The authors prove that a Rydberg-motivated two-body blockade Hamiltonian remains finitely gapped in the thermodynamic limit.
application_angle: A rigorous gap result supports the viability of blockade-engineered topological phases as robust quantum-memory or fault-tolerant hardware resources.

title: Generation of large-amplitude squeezed cat states with near-unity efficiency
abstract: The Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill encoding has emerged as a leading candidate for fault-tolerant quantum computation with continuous variables. For photonic architectures, the major challenge is preparing high-quality resource states, which can be deterministically synthesised from many large-amplitude cat states. Thus far, only modest-sized optical cat states have been prepared experimentally, and the implemented methods are highly probabilistic. We propose an all-optical scheme utilising quantum non-demolition interactions and photon-number measurements to prepare large-amplitude cat states with near-unity probability. Importantly, no particular photon-number outcome is postselected: all outcomes contribute to the accumulated photon number, with the protocol repeated until a required threshold is reached. We demonstrate that the scheme is robust to realistic levels of photon-loss, the dominant source of error in optical systems. Our results highlight the power of active Gaussian operations for state preparation and pave the way for efficient quantum error correction using bosonic codes.
one_liner: All-optical protocol prepares large-amplitude squeezed cat states with near-unity success using QND interactions and photon counting.
why_it_matters: Efficient large cat-state generation is a key bottleneck for photonic GKP and bosonic-code fault-tolerant quantum computing.
detailed_summary: The work proposes an all-optical state-preparation scheme for large-amplitude squeezed cat states. Instead of postselecting specific photon-number outcomes, every photon-count result contributes to an accumulated threshold, allowing the protocol to repeat until the desired resource is reached. The authors analyze realistic photon loss and argue that active Gaussian operations make the scheme robust enough for quantum-error-correction resource generation.
main_result: The protocol generates large-amplitude squeezed cat states with near-unity probability using QND interactions and photon-number measurements.
application_angle: This could reduce the overhead of preparing resource states for photonic GKP encodings and bosonic-code quantum error correction.

title: Quantum double lock-in detection via sequential orthogonal quantum mixing
abstract: High-precision measurement of oscillating signal is a ubiquitous issue in fundamental science and a critical task in practical technologies. In quantum metrology, quantum lock-in detection provide an efficient method for measuring such signal. In general, when the initial phase of the oscillating signal is unknown,quantum double lock-in detection can effectively extract complete information about the signal's amplitude, frequency, and initial phase. Conventional quantum double lock-in detection requires two individual quantum interferometry, each of which must undergo state preparation and readout. However, the time for state preparation and readout need not be negligible in practical experiments. In particular, the time for state preparation is longer than the time for sensing. To save experimental resources, it is challenging to achieve quantum double lock-in detection just via a single quantum interferometry while still extracting complete information about the signal's amplitude, frequency, and initial phase. Here, we present a general protocol for achieving a quantum double lock-in detection just via a single quantum interferometry under a sequential orthogonal periodic multipulse sequences. In particular, if the input state is a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state and two interaction-based operations are applied during interferometry, the measurement precisions for frequency, amplitude, and initial phase can both approach the Heisenberg limit. Our study paves a new way for measuring oscillating signals with a single quantum interferometry, and provides a feasible method for achieving Heisenberg-limited detection of alternating signals.
one_liner: Single-interferometer quantum double lock-in detection extracts amplitude, frequency, and phase via sequential orthogonal mixing.
why_it_matters: Reducing two lock-in interferometers to one can save preparation and readout overhead in practical quantum sensors for AC signals.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces a quantum double lock-in protocol based on sequential orthogonal periodic multipulse sequences within a single interferometry experiment. It targets oscillating signals with unknown initial phase, recovering amplitude, frequency, and phase without running two separate interferometers. With GHZ inputs and interaction-based operations, the analysis shows frequency, amplitude, and phase precisions approaching the Heisenberg limit.
main_result: The authors show complete AC-signal parameter estimation using one quantum interferometer rather than two separate lock-in measurements.
application_angle: The protocol is relevant for quantum sensors where state preparation and readout dominate the experimental duty cycle.

title: Layer codes as quantum memories: syndrome extraction, thresholds and idle robustness
abstract: Layer codes are three-dimensional local CSS codes of check weight at most six, obtained by quasi-concatenating a CSS input code with unrotated surface code patches. What is established about them describes the code, not the circuit that measures it. In this work, we evaluate them as active memories under circuit-level noise. Doing so first requires a syndrome extraction circuit, and the junction stabilizers that couple the patches rule out borrowing a surface code patch's CNOT schedule. We present a decoder-free scheduler that constrains hook propagation first and compresses depth afterwards, generate circuits for eighteen layer codes across four input codes, and compare them with surface codes of the same distance, simulated and decoded in the same way. The circuits lose no distance to hook errors on [[4,2,2]]-input codes wherever a circuit-distance proof is affordable, and reach a lower logical error rate than those of a general-purpose scheduler for CSS codes at roughly half its CNOT depth per round. Our primary family built from a [[4,2,2]] input code reaches a circuit-level threshold of $5.06(7)\times 10^{-3}$. The layer code outperforms the surface code in terms of idle robustness: at the same distance it tolerates an interval between syndrome extraction rounds 1.7-3.0 times longer than the rotated surface code. This comes at the cost of 1.7-5.0 times more operations per unit time and approximately five times more physical qubits, both per logical qubit. Finally, we model the cost of the beyond-2D cross-plane CNOTs that the construction demands, and find that their speed matters far more than their fidelity.
one_liner: Circuit-level study of 3D layer-code memories finds a 5.06e-3 threshold and stronger idle robustness than surface codes.
why_it_matters: Layer codes may trade more qubits and operations for longer tolerable idle intervals, useful for architectures with slow or costly rounds.
detailed_summary: The work develops syndrome-extraction circuits for 3D local CSS layer codes, where junction stabilizers prevent reuse of ordinary surface-code CNOT schedules. A decoder-free scheduler controls hook-error propagation and compresses circuit depth, then the authors simulate eighteen layer codes under circuit-level noise. The main [[4,2,2]]-input family reaches a threshold of 5.06(7)e-3 and tolerates 1.7-3.0 times longer idle intervals than rotated surface codes at the same distance, with higher qubit and operation costs.
main_result: Layer-code memory circuits achieve a circuit-level threshold of 5.06(7)e-3 and improved idle robustness relative to comparable surface codes.
application_angle: The results map a concrete hardware tradeoff for quantum memories in systems where idle time, cross-plane gates, and syndrome-cycle speed are limiting factors.

title: Optimal local recovery cannot alter critical orthogonality exponents in quantum spin environments
abstract: We prove a local amplitude-ratio bound for positive ground states and an explicit reverse comparison for fidelity under finite-region erasure. An exact lattice calculation for a connected critical Ising chain gives amplitude exponent $1/8$, preserved by arbitrary optimal control on any fixed spin set and, at the level of logarithmic exponents, on $o(\log N)$ spins. We derive the finite Cauchy product and its uniform strip asymptotics, and document exact two-spin optimization and an interferometric protocol for measuring the recovery. A separate finite-mediator theorem quantifies local compression and a decoder while retaining the rest of the environment exactly. We also give a ground-preparation Ramsey bound, counterexamples to stronger projected-state inferences, and independent full-Hamiltonian calculations.
one_liner: Local recovery operations cannot change critical orthogonality exponents in spin environments, even with optimized finite-region control.
why_it_matters: The result bounds how much local control can mitigate decoherence-like critical environment effects in sensing and interferometry settings.
detailed_summary: The authors prove bounds showing that optimal local recovery on a finite spin region cannot alter critical orthogonality exponents for positive ground states. For a connected critical Ising chain, an exact calculation gives an amplitude exponent of 1/8 that survives arbitrary optimal control on fixed spin sets and, logarithmically, on sublogarithmic-size regions. The paper also proposes an interferometric protocol to measure the recovery and analyzes finite-mediator compression and decoding.
main_result: The paper proves that local recovery cannot change the critical orthogonality exponent governing ground-state fidelity loss.
application_angle: This clarifies fundamental limits for locally correcting environment-induced contrast loss in Ramsey-style quantum sensing experiments.

title: Boron vacancies in bulk h-BN created by high-energy He+ irradiation
abstract: While color centers in diamond and other three-dimensional crystals are nowadays key elements of several types of sensors, color centers in two-dimensional materials are rapidly developing and promise high-tech applications. One of the interesting centers in 2D materials is the negatively charged boron vacancy in hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN), which has already shown some potential for magnetometry, but the reliable creation of boron vacancies remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate the fabrication of negatively charged boron vacancy color centers in bulk h-BN via implantation of helium ions at ~1 MeV, as confirmed by characteristic photoluminescence and optically detected magnetic resonance. The resonance has a width of 180 MHz and exhibits the expected Zeeman shift of the resonance lines. The depth of the color center along the c-axis of the h-BN crystal was measured and compared with predictions from Stopping and Range of Ions in Matter modeling. The experimental value and the modeled prediction are consistent within the reported uncertainties, as their 1σ intervals overlap, although the experiment shows a greater depth and a wider distribution.
one_liner: MeV He+ irradiation creates negatively charged boron-vacancy centers in bulk h-BN verified by PL and ODMR.
why_it_matters: Reliable vacancy creation in h-BN is a practical step toward 2D-material quantum sensors and integrated photonic sensing platforms.
detailed_summary: The study demonstrates fabrication of negatively charged boron-vacancy color centers in bulk hexagonal boron nitride using approximately 1 MeV helium-ion implantation. The centers are confirmed through characteristic photoluminescence and optically detected magnetic resonance, with a reported 180 MHz resonance linewidth and Zeeman-shifting resonance lines. Depth measurements along the crystal c-axis are compared with SRIM simulations and found consistent within overlapping one-sigma uncertainties, though the measured distribution is deeper and broader.
main_result: The authors create V_B^- centers in bulk h-BN by high-energy He+ irradiation and verify their optical and spin signatures by PL and ODMR.
application_angle: Controlled creation of h-BN spin defects supports scalable magnetometry and hybrid photonic-sensor devices based on layered materials.

title: Exact Maximum Likelihood Decoding beyond Treewidth via Rank-Decomposition Dynamic Programming
abstract: Maximum-likelihood decoding provides an optimal decoding strategy for quantum error correction under stochastic Pauli noise. However, computing logical-class probabilities is challenging, and the leading exact tensor-network contraction requires time exponential in treewidth. In this work, we introduce a new decoding algorithm based on rank-decomposition dynamic programming (Rank DP). We express decoding partition functions with independent local fault factors as quadratic sums of powers and apply Rank DP. The resulting exact evaluator has arithmetic complexity polynomial in the input size and exponential in the Tanner graph's rank-width with respect to the fault partition, including decomposition construction. After Gaussian elimination, it gives polynomial-time decoding for punctured quantum Reed-Muller codes and a Steane-concatenated family with growing distance under independent single-qubit Pauli noise. Standard contraction of the corresponding tensor networks requires superpolynomial time. A nonnegative realization gives relative floating-point error bounds under explicit arithmetic assumptions. Numerical experiments demonstrate runtime advantages over the tested tensor-network implementations on selected code-capacity and circuit-level instances, with full likelihood evaluation for Reed-Muller codes up to $1{,}023$ qubits. We further use these likelihoods to learn circuit noise parameters from syndromes, evaluate rare postselection probabilities, and quantify decoder optimality gaps. Our work opens new avenues for exploiting algebraic structure in quantum decoding and noise characterization.
one_liner: Rank-decomposition dynamic programming enables exact maximum-likelihood quantum decoding beyond treewidth-limited tensor contraction.
why_it_matters: Exact decoding and likelihood evaluation become tractable for algebraically structured codes, supporting both QEC benchmarking and noise characterization.
detailed_summary: The paper reformulates logical-class likelihood evaluation for Pauli-noise quantum error correction as quadratic sums of powers and solves them with rank-decomposition dynamic programming. Its complexity is exponential in a rank-width parameter rather than tensor-network treewidth, giving polynomial-time decoding for selected punctured Reed-Muller and concatenated Steane families. Numerics show full likelihood evaluation up to 1,023-qubit Reed-Muller instances and applications to syndrome-based noise-parameter learning and postselection estimates.
main_result: An exact decoder evaluates full logical likelihoods efficiently on code families where tested tensor-network contractions become superpolynomial.
application_angle: The method can help calibrate and benchmark fault-tolerant hardware by giving exact decoder references and learned noise parameters.

title: Thermodynamics of Ahn--Doherty--Landahl Continuous Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Continuous quantum error correction (CQEC) replaces discrete syndrome measurements and recovery operations with continuous syndrome extraction and real-time Hamiltonian feedback. Here we investigate the thermodynamic resources required by this process by formulating measurement-based continuous quantum error correction as an information engine. We distinguish the system-side power associated with energy transfer between the feedback field and the protected system from the controller-side power associated with the feedback Hamiltonian. The framework is first developed for the one-qubit Ahn-Doherty-Landahl (ADL) protocol and subsequently extended to the three-qubit repetition code under continuous stabilizer monitoring. Numerical simulations show that increasing the feedback strength improves the steady-state fidelity and reduces the conditional-state entropy, while both energetic contributions continue to increase in magnitude after the fidelity begins to saturate. These results expose a direct tradeoff between logical stabilization and the energetic resources required for continuous feedback, closely related to previously established energy--precision tradeoffs in quantum measurement and quantum-Zeno stabilization.
one_liner: Continuous QEC is analyzed as an information engine with explicit energy costs for measurement-driven feedback stabilization.
why_it_matters: It quantifies the resource cost of always-on error correction, a practical constraint for autonomous or continuously monitored quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The work models Ahn-Doherty-Landahl continuous quantum error correction using thermodynamic power flows associated with the protected system and the controller feedback Hamiltonian. It treats both a one-qubit protocol and a continuously monitored three-qubit repetition code. Simulations show fidelity and conditional-entropy improvements with stronger feedback, while energetic costs keep rising after fidelity begins to saturate.
main_result: The study demonstrates a quantitative tradeoff between logical-state stabilization and feedback energy consumption in continuous QEC.
application_angle: These metrics are relevant for designing scalable autonomous QEC controllers where power, cooling, and feedback strength are engineering limits.

title: Phase-sensitive avalanche quantum sensing of sub-shot-noise fields
abstract: Avalanche-based detection of small perturbations is commonplace in precision measurement devices from Geiger counters to single-photon avalanche detectors. Here, we expand this principle to sensing of light waves below the quantum shot noise limit, demonstrating numerically how atomic clouds trapped in photonic cavities can exhibit non-perturbative sensitivity to changes in the cavity field when the cavity mode is tuned to a parity-prohibited transition. We find that, when pumped by a continuous-wave laser, the atomic cloud creates emissions which amplify the initially sub-shot-noise fluctuation by two orders of magnitude. Crucially, this amplification is broadly tunable with respect to frequency and independent of atomic energy structure. Even more strikingly, our amplification mechanism preserves the phase imparted on the atoms by the original ultra-weak light wave, marking a qualitative improvement over conventional protocols. Our finding has implications for both quantum state characterization and detection of weak classical signals.
one_liner: Cavity-trapped atomic clouds are proposed to avalanche-amplify sub-shot-noise optical fields while preserving phase information.
why_it_matters: Phase-preserving amplification of ultra-weak fields could improve quantum optical sensing and state characterization below shot-noise levels.
detailed_summary: The paper numerically studies atoms trapped in photonic cavities tuned near a parity-prohibited transition, where small cavity-field perturbations trigger non-perturbative emission responses. Under continuous-wave pumping, the atomic cloud amplifies initially sub-shot-noise fluctuations by roughly two orders of magnitude. Unlike many avalanche-style detectors, the mechanism preserves the phase originally imprinted on the atoms by the weak light field.
platform_or_system: atomic cloud in a photonic cavity
main_result: Numerical simulations show broadly tunable, phase-sensitive amplification of ultra-weak optical fluctuations below the shot-noise scale.
application_angle: The approach targets weak classical-signal detection and quantum-state characterization where retaining phase is essential.

title: Scaling Laws of Quantum Networks: An Entanglement Transport Framework
abstract: As quantum networks move toward multi-user architectures, a central question is how the performance of entanglement distribution scales with the numbers of network nodes $N$ and active users $M$, yet existing studies use different objectives, resource assumptions, and normalizations. To account for delivery distance under multi-user demand, we define entanglement transport, which weights each delivered Bell pair meeting a fixed fidelity threshold by its endpoint separation. In a two-layer framework, (i) a resource layer measures capacity per activation slot under different aggregation regimes, and (ii) a physical layer measures service per second under implementation constraints. For matched implementations with a bounded number of activation slots per second, asymptotic-aggregation capacity sets a service ceiling, whereas achievable service must be established separately. On expanding honeycomb lattices with one random session, fixed-window entanglement-percolation constructions achieve $Θ(N^{-1})$ entanglement transport per activation slot below their thresholds and $Θ(\sqrt N)$ above them. For homogeneous chains, asymptotic aggregation exceeds fixed-window capacity by a factor $Θ(N^2/M)$, and in spatial expansion a noisy physical implementation achieves $Θ(M/N)$ service per second. These examples show that entanglement-transport scaling depends not only on connectivity but also on resource aggregation and physical implementation. The framework provides a common basis on which quantum-network scaling laws can be established.
one_liner: A transport metric is introduced to compare quantum-network scaling by weighting delivered Bell pairs by endpoint separation.
why_it_matters: The framework clarifies how connectivity, aggregation assumptions, and physical implementation jointly determine usable entanglement-distribution scaling.
detailed_summary: The paper defines entanglement transport as delivered Bell pairs above a fidelity threshold weighted by endpoint distance, separating resource-layer capacity from physical-layer service. It derives scaling examples for expanding honeycomb lattices, homogeneous chains, and noisy spatial implementations. Results show sharp dependence on aggregation windows, user count, network size, and implementation limits rather than topology alone.
main_result: The work provides scaling laws showing when entanglement transport ranges from suppressed behavior to growing service, depending on regime and architecture.
application_angle: This gives network designers a common metric for comparing repeater, routing, and resource-allocation strategies in future quantum internets.

title: Quantum--classical break-even in electronic dynamics of macrocyclic molecules
abstract: Here we demonstrate quantum--classical break-even for chemical dynamics applications, reaching useful accuracy with a quantum-hardware wall-clock time comparable to that estimated for practical classical computing resources. Specifically, we construct a quantum workflow for electronic dynamics based on tensor-network circuit compression leveraging spatial locality, extending circuit compression beyond one-dimensional open-boundary systems. This enables application of the workflow to problems that are hardware-native but classically hard. The workflow targets one-dimensional periodic Hamiltonians: circuits classically optimized only for short-time evolution within a small spatial region can be replicated in both space and time to construct long-time dynamics of the full system without classically simulating the corresponding large-scale evolution. We apply the workflow to cyclic conjugated macrocycles with rotational periodicity, 12-qubit benzene and 120-qubit [60]annulene, by embedding their electronic structure onto loops of IBM quantum processors. For the annulene, the quantum-processing-unit (QPU) wall-clock times for hole-doped nonequilibrium dynamics became comparable to the estimated wall-clock time of two classical methods, Majorana propagation and matrix-product-state time evolution based on the time-dependent variational principle; this corresponds to tens to hundreds of compute nodes depending on the task (36 CPU cores per node), even assuming ideal scaling, bringing the quantum calculation into a wall-clock-time regime comparable to conventional parallel high-performance-computing resources. We also show a situation in which a hybrid quantum--classical calculation is a reasonable choice in terms of both accuracy and computational time. These results show that quantum hardware can become a realistic computational option for chemically relevant electronic dynamics.
one_liner: IBM processors are used for electronic dynamics of cyclic molecules, reaching quantum-classical wall-clock break-even estimates for annulene.
why_it_matters: It reports an application-oriented hardware workflow where quantum execution time becomes comparable to serious classical HPC estimates.
detailed_summary: The authors build a quantum workflow for periodic one-dimensional electronic Hamiltonians using tensor-network circuit compression that exploits locality and rotational structure. Short-time, local circuits are optimized classically, then replicated across space and time for larger dynamics without classically simulating the full evolution. The workflow is applied to 12-qubit benzene and 120-qubit [60]annulene mapped onto IBM processor loops, with annulene QPU wall-clock times comparable to estimated parallel classical approaches.
main_result: The study demonstrates chemically relevant nonequilibrium electronic dynamics with QPU wall-clock time comparable to estimated classical HPC runtimes for selected tasks.
application_angle: It supports near-term hybrid quantum chemistry workflows where hardware-native structure can offset classical simulation costs.

title: Theory of spacetime quantum fault tolerance
abstract: We present a unified algebraic theory of Clifford spacetime quantum fault tolerance, which underpins universal fault-tolerant quantum computation. We construct a spacetime chain complex from a tensor network representation of a circuit that encodes fault propagation, detector syndromes, and logical actions through the associated gauge and stabilizer structure. We show that this theory (1) unifies various formulations of quantum fault tolerance including spacetime codes, Gottesman's gadget framework, fault complexes, and ZX calculus; (2) connects spacetime distances to the gadget-level correctness properties in Gottesman's formalism; (3) naturally accommodates a range of fault models, in particular phenomenological and circuit-level models, bringing these often separately formulated descriptions into a common algebraic framework through different tensor decompositions and fault assignments; and (4) recovers many known fault tolerance constructions and results as special cases, including repeated syndrome extraction, correlated detectors for transversal and fold-transversal gates, Steane- and Knill-type syndrome extraction gadgets, and single-shot error correction.
one_liner: A unified algebraic framework describes Clifford spacetime fault tolerance across circuits, detectors, logical actions, and faults.
why_it_matters: A common formalism can make hardware-level fault-tolerance analysis more systematic across circuit-level and phenomenological noise models.
detailed_summary: The paper constructs a spacetime chain complex from tensor-network representations of fault-tolerant circuits. This complex tracks fault propagation, detector syndromes, gauge and stabilizer structure, and logical actions in a unified algebraic language. It connects spacetime distances to gadget-correctness conditions and recovers known constructions such as repeated syndrome extraction, Steane- and Knill-type gadgets, transversal gates, and single-shot error correction.
main_result: The work unifies multiple formulations of quantum fault tolerance under a spacetime algebraic theory supporting different fault assignments and tensor decompositions.
application_angle: It can guide rigorous design and comparison of fault-tolerant hardware protocols under realistic detector and circuit-level error models.

title: No-go theorems for dual Hamiltonians of Non-Abelian Lattice Gauge Theories
abstract: Hamiltonian simulations of lattice gauge theories promise new insights into the inner workings of QCD. The rapid development of quantum computing hardware suggests that large scale simulations may soon become feasible. However, no efficient formulation suitable for simulations near the continuum limit is currently known for the non-Abelian case, and existing candidates typically feature long range interactions in the electric part of the Hamiltonian. We prove that such non- localities are unavoidable when the gauge configuration is reparametrised while preserving both the number of degrees of freedom and the fundamental commutation relations. We then attempt to mitigate this by introducing additional gauge links alongside additional constraints. Although this approach is successful in U(1), we prove that the corresponding construction is inconsistent for non-Abelian lattice gauge theories.
one_liner: Proves structural obstructions to local dual Hamiltonians for non-Abelian lattice gauge theories near continuum simulation regimes.
why_it_matters: Clarifies when hardware-efficient gauge-theory mappings are impossible, shaping realistic quantum-simulation architectures for QCD-like models.
detailed_summary: The paper proves that reparametrizing non-Abelian lattice gauge configurations while preserving degrees of freedom and canonical commutation relations necessarily produces nonlocal electric Hamiltonian terms. It also studies an auxiliary-link construction that works for U(1) but is shown inconsistent for non-Abelian theories.
