By processing the measurement window in successive time chunks, the networks exploit temporal structure and update classification scores as data arrive, rather than waiting until the end of the readout window. The spiking networks outperform matched-filter discrimination and approach the accuracy of a full-trace artificial neural network. Beyond reaching the performance of artificial neural networks, the key advantage of SNNs is that they provide a streaming, time-resolved estimate of the qubit state that evolves as the readout signal is acquired. Using quantisation-aware training and hls4ml synthesis, we further demonstrate that each FPGA inference update can be completed before the next readout chunk arrives. These results establish spiking neural networks as a promising route to low-latency, real-time qubit readout on FPGA hardware, with broader implications for time-critical quantum-control and scientific-inference applications.
one_liner: Demonstrates spiking neural-network discriminators for streaming, low-latency superconducting-qubit readout on FPGA hardware.
why_it_matters: It targets a real hardware bottleneck: fast state assignment for feedback, calibration, and error correction in quantum processors.
detailed_summary: The authors introduce SNN discriminators that process multiplexed superconducting-qubit readout traces in successive time chunks and update classification scores as data arrive. The SNNs outperform matched filtering and approach full-trace artificial neural-network accuracy while preserving time-resolved streaming outputs. With quantization-aware training and hls4ml synthesis, they show FPGA inference updates can finish before the next readout chunk arrives.
main_result: Spiking neural networks provide accurate streaming qubit-state assignment with FPGA-compatible per-chunk latency.
application_angle: This is directly relevant to real-time feedback, adaptive calibration, and low-latency decoding in superconducting quantum processors.

title: Quantum impurity models: easy at equilibrium, universal in motion
abstract: A quantum impurity model describes a small interacting subsystem embedded into a large bath of free fermions. Here we study the computational complexity of calculating the ground energy, thermal equilibrium, and dynamical properties of these models. Our work reveals a sharp contrast: equilibrium properties can be efficiently approximated by classical means, whereas time evolution can implement a universal quantum computation. More precisely, let $H$ be the Hamiltonian of an impurity model with $n$ fermionic modes and a constant-size impurity. We show that: (1) the ground energy of $H$ can be approximated to additive error $\varepsilon$ by a classical algorithm with runtime $\textsf{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon)$, improving on the quasi-polynomial runtime of the best previously known algorithm; (2) at inverse temperature $β$, the Helmholtz free energy and a classical description of the thermofield double state can be computed to precision $\varepsilon$ in time $\textsf{poly}(n,β,1/\varepsilon)$; (3) simulating the time evolution $e^{-iHt}$ is $\textsf{BQP}$-complete, for $H$ that is time-independent and has a fixed, constant impurity size. Our algorithms exploit exponential suppression of multi-particle bath excitations in a basis organized by energy scale and Krylov depth. Our universality construction realizes a stationary quantum processor whose program arrives in a stream of freely propagating fermions.
one_liner: Finds impurity models are classically tractable at equilibrium but become BQP-complete under time evolution.
why_it_matters: It clarifies which impurity-model workloads are easy for classical simulation and which can act as universal quantum hardware dynamics.
detailed_summary: The paper studies impurity models with n fermionic modes and a constant-size interacting impurity. It gives polynomial-time classical algorithms for ground energy, Helmholtz free energy, and thermofield-double descriptions at finite temperature, improving prior quasi-polynomial behavior. In contrast, it proves that simulating time-independent real-time evolution is BQP-complete using a construction where a program is carried by freely propagating fermions.
main_result: Equilibrium observables of constant-impurity models are classically efficient, while their dynamics can realize universal quantum computation.
application_angle: The result guides quantum-simulation hardware proposals by separating classically simulable regimes from dynamically universal regimes.

title: Random Quantum Circuits Beyond Moment Matching
abstract: Random quantum circuits aim to efficiently reproduce the statistical properties of ideal random quantum evolution. One approach is to construct approximate unitary designs, which match the moments of Haar-random unitaries up to a prescribed order with controlled error. In this work, we establish quantitative guarantees for how accurately these designs reproduce the full distributions of individual output probabilities. We show that, for every strong $\varepsilon$-approximate unitary $k$-design on $n$ qubits, the distribution of each individual output probability is within $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{2^n}{k(k+2^n)}}+\varepsilon\right)$ in Kolmogorov distance of the finite-dimensional Porter-Thomas distribution, a beta distribution with parameters $1$ and $2^n-1$. This bound is optimal up to constant factors, implying that a substantially better uniform bound requires additional structure. We further show that local invariance yields an exponential improvement in the dependence on $k$, with guarantees also in the stronger metric of total variation: every strong $\varepsilon$-approximate unitary $k$-design invariant under unitary translations acting on $\log k+O(1)$ qubits achieves error $2^{-Ω(k)}+O(\varepsilon)$ in Kolmogorov distance and $2^{-Ω(k)}+O(\varepsilon\log(2/\varepsilon))$ in total variation distance. These results identify both the distributional accuracy guaranteed by moment matching and the additional structure that substantially improves it. As an application, we show that if the marginal distribution of each output probability of a strong approximate design is within Kolmogorov distance $η$ of its Haar counterpart, then the expected Shannon entropy of the output distribution differs from its Haar value by $O(\sqrtη)$.
one_liner: Quantifies when approximate unitary designs reproduce Porter-Thomas output-probability statistics beyond moment matching.
why_it_matters: Gives sharper guarantees for random-circuit benchmarking and entropy estimates, clarifying what design order alone can and cannot certify.
detailed_summary: The paper proves quantitative bounds connecting strong approximate unitary k-designs to full marginal distributions of output probabilities. It shows generic moment matching reaches Porter-Thomas statistics only up to an optimal Kolmogorov-distance scale, while additional local invariance can improve the error exponentially in k. The results also bound deviations in expected output Shannon entropy from the Haar value.
main_result: Strong approximate k-designs are shown to approximate finite-dimensional Porter-Thomas output statistics with optimal generic bounds and stronger guarantees under local invariance.
application_angle: This supports more rigorous interpretation of random-circuit experiments, entropy diagnostics, and hardware benchmarking protocols.

title: One-Shot any Code
abstract: We first provide a simple proof showing that any single-shot code is self-correcting. We then show that any $[[n,k]]$ CSS quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) code can be transformed into an $[[nm,k]]$ CSS QLDPC code with single-shot (SS) quantum error correction and an efficient local decoder which runs in $O(\log m)$ parallel time. Below a constant threshold $p_{\rm RG}>0$ for joint local stochastic physical and measurement noise, the logical failure probability over $T$ correction rounds is bounded by \begin{equation*} O(T n)\exp[-Ω(m^α)] \end{equation*} for a constant $α>0$; we say that the \textit{threshold} is $p_{\rm RG}$ and \textit{error suppression} is $Ω(m^α)$. Moreover, if the input code is equipped with a single-shot decoder with threshold $p_c>0$ and error suppression $Ω(n^β)$, then the output code \textit{enhances} the error suppression to $Ω(m^α n^β)$, while maintaining the decoder-independent threshold $p_{\rm RG}$, and thus \textit{enhanced} if $p_c < p_{\rm RG}$.
one_liner: Transforms any CSS QLDPC code into a single-shot code with efficient local decoding and scalable error suppression.
why_it_matters: Single-shot correction reduces repeated syndrome-measurement overhead, a key practical bottleneck for fault-tolerant quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The work proves that any single-shot code is self-correcting and gives a construction turning an [[n,k]] CSS QLDPC code into an [[nm,k]] CSS QLDPC code with single-shot error correction. The decoder runs in O(log m) parallel time and tolerates joint local stochastic physical and measurement noise below a constant threshold. It also shows how an input single-shot decoder's error suppression can be enhanced multiplicatively.
main_result: Any CSS QLDPC code can be converted into a single-shot CSS QLDPC code with constant threshold and exp[-Omega(m^alpha)] logical-failure suppression over repeated rounds.
application_angle: The construction is relevant for reducing syndrome-extraction latency and measurement repetition in scalable fault-tolerant architectures.

title: A provable quantum advantage for approximate optimization via decoded quantum interferometry
abstract: Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is a novel paradigm for tackling approximate optimization problems on quantum computers. This framework comes with strong performance guarantees and exploits a well-established duality between optimization and coding theory. A central question, however, is whether DQI can actually provably outperform all polynomial-time classical algorithms. In this work, we establish such an advantage in an oracle setting: we consider an optimization task called folded optimal polynomial intersection (folded OPI), where the acceptance sets are chosen randomly and accessed through membership oracles. We establish a strict gap between the approximation ratio achievable by any polynomial-time classical algorithm and the approximation ratio achieved by the DQI algorithm. Our proof builds on Jordan et al.'s DQI framework for approximate optimization and extends the classical lower-bound method underlying Yamakawa and Zhandry's exact-search oracle separation to approximation. Building on recent developments by Sun and Wootters, Horinaga and Yamakawa, and Jo, we further show that a modified version of the DQI algorithm achieves a strictly higher score guarantee on typical sampled folded OPI instances. As a concrete example, for code rate $0.3$, DQI achieves expected scores of approximately $0.85$. In contrast, exceeding the classical threshold of $0.65$ by any fixed amount with constant probability on sampled instances requires super-polynomially many classical membership queries.
one_liner: Proves an oracle-setting quantum advantage for decoded quantum interferometry on approximate optimization tasks.
why_it_matters: It gives a rigorous separation where a quantum algorithm beats polynomial-time classical membership-query algorithms in approximation quality.
detailed_summary: The paper studies folded optimal polynomial intersection, an oracle optimization problem built from random acceptance sets. It proves that decoded quantum interferometry achieves approximation scores beyond what polynomial-time classical algorithms can reach with constant probability. For code rate 0.3, the authors report expected DQI scores near 0.85, while classically exceeding 0.65 by a fixed amount requires super-polynomially many queries.
main_result: DQI is shown to provide a provable approximation advantage over polynomial-time classical algorithms in a membership-oracle model.
application_angle: The result strengthens the case for quantum optimization primitives with coding-theoretic structure, though the demonstrated advantage is oracle-based rather than device-level.

title: Beyond Light Cones: State Preparation Complexity in Quantum Spin Glasses
abstract: We introduce a method for studying state preparation complexity in dense quantum $p$-spin Hamiltonians on $n$ qubits, going beyond bounds based only on circuit lightcones. The key input is the class's effective profile complexity, which is derived from the metric entropy of its Pauli profiles. These profiles record expectations of all Pauli operators supported on exactly $p$ qubits. Classes with uniformly bounded quadratic effective profile complexity remain separated from the ground-state energy by a positive multiple of $\sqrt n$ for sufficiently large fixed $p$. At subquadratic effective profile complexity, the class cannot outperform a suitable benchmark class at leading order, with product states providing a universal benchmark. The proof combines an adaptation of a nonsymmetric quantum de Finetti theorem of Berta et al. (arXiv:1810.12197) with Gaussian process entropy bounds. Applying this framework, we show that attaining near-ground-state energy requires $Ω(n^2/\log n)$ one- and two-qubit gates, even with arbitrary discardable ancillas. We also obtain depth-width tradeoffs, entanglement-depth and matrix product state bond-dimension lower bounds, and obstructions for both orientations at every fixed level of Parham's magic hierarchy (arXiv:2504.19966), with total circuit width $O(n)$. In first-level reverse magic, a shallow circuit is followed by an unrestricted Clifford circuit. The latter can spread local observables across the system, preventing a direct application of small-lightcone bounds. For this first-level class, our bounds also allow arbitrarily many clean ancillas at fixed shallow-circuit depth. A sharper benchmark shows that Clifford+$T$ circuits with $o(n)$ $T$-gates have no leading-order energy advantage over product stabilizer states, even with unrestricted Clifford operations and arbitrary discardable ancillas.
one_liner: Establishes strong lower bounds on preparing near-ground states of dense quantum spin-glass Hamiltonians.
why_it_matters: The bounds clarify when shallow, low-magic, or limited-entanglement quantum hardware cannot efficiently prepare hard many-body states.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces effective profile complexity, based on metric entropy of Pauli expectation profiles, to study dense quantum p-spin Hamiltonians beyond lightcone arguments. It proves that near-ground-state preparation requires Omega(n^2/log n) one- and two-qubit gates, even with discardable ancillas. The framework also yields depth-width, entanglement-depth, matrix-product-state, and Clifford+T magic-resource lower bounds.
main_result: Near-ground-state preparation for dense quantum spin glasses requires at least Omega(n^2/log n) one- and two-qubit gates under broad circuit models.
application_angle: These limits help benchmark variational algorithms and hardware-efficient ansatzes for quantum optimization and many-body simulation.

title: Robust exponential lower bounds for fermionic and bosonic Gaussian ranks
abstract: The power and limitations of classical simulation are central to understanding quantum computational advantages. A leading simulation paradigm is based on coherent decomposition into classically tractable free states where the decomposition rank determines the simulation complexity. Proving strong lower bounds on this number is a notoriously difficult and mathematically rich problem, as exemplified by the qubit stabilizer rank problem. Here, we study the Gaussian version of this problem in both bosonic and fermionic systems and establish robust exponential lower bounds on Gaussian rank. In particular, we prove that for every pure non-Gaussian state on finitely many modes, with definite parity in the fermionic case, the approximate border Gaussian rank of its tensor powers grows at least exponentially at any fixed norm error below one. Our proofs combine reduction to four modes with Majorana spectral bounds for fermions, and Gaussian postselection with an entropy-based rank bound for bosons. As concrete examples, we derive explicit exponential lower bounds for the four-mode fermionic GHZ state and the bosonic single-photon state. The bosonic results require no assumption on the energy of the target state. Our results show that non-Gaussianity universally entails exponential Gaussian decomposition complexity, setting fundamental limitations on decomposition-based classical simulation of bosonic and fermionic systems.
one_liner: Proves universal robust exponential lower bounds on Gaussian decomposition rank for non-Gaussian bosonic and fermionic states.
why_it_matters: It sets fundamental limits on Gaussian-rank simulation strategies for photonic and fermionic quantum systems with non-Gaussian resources.
detailed_summary: The paper studies decomposition of quantum states into classically tractable Gaussian states for both bosonic and fermionic systems. It proves that tensor powers of any pure non-Gaussian state, with definite parity in the fermionic case, require approximate border Gaussian rank growing exponentially at fixed norm error below one. Explicit examples include four-mode fermionic GHZ states and bosonic single-photon states, without an energy assumption for the bosonic result.
main_result: Any pure non-Gaussian state has tensor powers with robust exponential approximate Gaussian-rank growth at fixed error below one.
application_angle: The result delineates when non-Gaussian photonic resources become intrinsically hard for decomposition-based classical simulation.

title: From Permutation Symmetry to Communication Bounds and Additivity
abstract: Correlations across channel uses can improve quantum communication rates, making optimization over arbitrarily large blocks a central difficulty in determining quantum capacity. We show how full permutation invariance limits this advantage for every finite-dimensional memoryless channel. The optimized coherent information per use converges to the single-use maximum and consequently attains its supremum at a finite block length. Thus finite-block superadditivity remains possible, while the asymptotic optimization reduces to a single channel use. We also establish a strong converse for pure-source entanglement generation with permutation-invariant inputs: at any fixed rate above the single-use coherent-information maximum, the fidelity tends to zero. Beyond these communication bounds, we identify a common structure underlying completely bounded norms and the sandwiched Rényi channel quantities governing discrimination against a replacer and entanglement-assisted communication. De Finetti reduction and permutation covariance yield systematic alternative proofs of their known multiplicativity and additivity results within a shared variational framework. We further show that, for permutation-invariant inputs, correlations cannot sustain an asymptotic reduction in output entropy per use below the single-use minimum. This entropy limit holds for Rényi orders greater than one and for the von Neumann entropy, extending the role of symmetry from communication bounds to the control of output entropy.
one_liner: Shows permutation symmetry constrains asymptotic quantum-channel correlations, yielding finite-block communication bounds.
why_it_matters: It reduces certain symmetric quantum-capacity and entropy optimizations to controlled finite-block or single-use quantities.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes finite-dimensional memoryless channels under fully permutation-invariant inputs across channel uses. It proves that optimized coherent information per use converges to the single-use maximum and that the supremum is attained at finite block length. It also establishes a strong converse for pure-source entanglement generation and uses de Finetti reduction to recover multiplicativity and additivity structures for channel quantities.
main_result: For permutation-invariant inputs, asymptotic coherent-information optimization collapses to the single-use maximum, with finite-block attainment and strong-converse behavior.
application_angle: The bounds simplify capacity analysis for symmetric communication protocols and clarify when correlated channel uses cannot sustain asymptotic gains.

title: Homological Thresholds in Randomly Monitored Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
abstract: Random projective measurements are an effective tool to model the interlinked phenomenology of monitoring, inferring, and decoding highly entangled states such as quantum error-correcting codes. At the same time, the study of such monitored dynamics has opened a new arena for critical phenomena, renewing longstanding questions in disordered statistical mechanics, including percolation, random-bond models, and Nishimori physics. Here we investigate the robustness of stabilizer quantum error-correcting codes under a single round of independently sampled single-qubit Pauli measurements and demonstrate that their threshold behavior falls into two broad categories - geometric and homological percolation transitions, with the toric code and color code being the principal examples for each class. We establish the distinct character of these two threshold theories by analyzing the logical-support criteria of these codes and by providing numerical estimates of their respective critical exponents obtained from optimized stabilizer simulations of large-scale systems with over one million qubits. Our framework extends to non-CSS, subsystem, higher-dimensional, and Floquet stabilizer codes and allows us to determine their respective threshold phase diagrams. We exemplify how the latter provide quantitative and qualitative guidance for the computationally more demanding problems of tunable learning and maximum-likelihood decoding. As a practical application of our framework, we discuss the robustness of the gross code.
one_liner: Classifies monitored stabilizer-code thresholds into geometric and homological percolation regimes using million-qubit simulations.
why_it_matters: Gives hardware-relevant guidance for how stabilizer memories tolerate measurement loss and informs decoder design for large-scale quantum processors.
detailed_summary: The paper studies a single round of independently sampled single-qubit Pauli measurements on stabilizer quantum error-correcting codes. It separates threshold behavior into geometric and homological percolation transitions, using toric and color codes as representative cases. Optimized stabilizer simulations exceeding one million qubits provide critical-exponent estimates and threshold phase diagrams across CSS, non-CSS, subsystem, higher-dimensional, and Floquet codes.
main_result: The main result is a threshold framework that distinguishes geometric from homological percolation failure modes and predicts robustness for broad stabilizer-code families.
application_angle: The phase diagrams can guide practical code selection, tunable learning, and maximum-likelihood decoding under realistic measurement-induced erasure or monitoring processes.

title: Gap-Protected Heisenberg-Limited Squeezing with Locally Interacting Multi-Level Spins
abstract: We demonstrate a general mechanism to generate scalable, metrologically useful entanglement in the form of generalized spin squeezing in multi-level (qudit) spin systems with power-law interactions. We demonstrate this for spin-changing dynamics, extending the physics of spin-nematic squeezing known from spinor BECs to spatially extended lattice geometries. In the absence of all-to-all connectivity, the dynamics generally suffers from leakage into non-collective finite-momentum modes, destroying Heisenberg scaling. We show that introducing local $\mathfrak{su}(D)$ exchange interactions establishes an energy gap that protects the fully symmetric collective manifold, suppressing non-collective excitations, and achieving Heisenberg scaling $ξ^2\propto1/N$ in one to three dimensions for any power-law exponent. We provide an analytical understanding of the mechanism via the analysis of the Bogoliubov excitation spectrum, and demonstrate its effectiveness via numerical simulations of the quantum many-body dynamics. Our findings more broadly apply to other spin-squeezing Hamiltonians, and directly generalize to larger internal spin dimensions. Our results provide a practical pathway towards scalable Heisenberg-limited qudit entanglement generation in experimental platforms such as arrays of (polar) molecules, magnetic atoms, and Rydberg atoms realizing multi-level spin systems.
one_liner: Shows gap-protected qudit spin squeezing can recover Heisenberg scaling in locally interacting power-law spin arrays.
why_it_matters: Provides a route to scalable metrological entanglement without requiring all-to-all connectivity, relevant to neutral atoms, molecules, and magnetic atoms.
detailed_summary: The work proposes local su(D) exchange interactions as a protection mechanism for generalized spin squeezing in multi-level spin systems. Without the gap, spin-changing dynamics leaks into finite-momentum modes and loses collective Heisenberg scaling. Analytical Bogoliubov spectra and many-body simulations show that the exchange gap suppresses non-collective excitations and enables xi^2 proportional to 1/N in one, two, and three dimensions.
main_result: The main result is a gap-protection mechanism that preserves fully symmetric collective squeezing dynamics and achieves Heisenberg-limited scaling for power-law interacting qudit systems.
application_angle: This is directly relevant to precision sensing and quantum hardware platforms based on polar molecules, magnetic atoms, and Rydberg-atom arrays.

title: Investigating entanglement dynamics with dynamical decoupling together with initial qubit-reservoir correlations
abstract: We study the exact entanglement dynamics of two qubits coupled to a common bosonic reservoir through a pure dephasing interaction. We ask how this dynamics changes when the qubits and the reservoir already share correlations before the qubit state is prepared. In that case the system and reservoir first interact for a long time and settle into a joint equilibrium state. Only afterward is the qubit pair projected onto the desired state by a local measurement. For an Ohmic spectral density we obtain the exact reduced two qubit dynamics. Using the Wootters concurrence we show that initial correlations always speed up entanglement sudden death relative to the factorized case, and that this gap grows quadratically with the coupling strength in the weak-to-moderate coupling regime. Finally we show that a symmetric sequence of periodic π pulses applied to both qubits extends the entanglement lifetime close to a factor of seven over the range of pulse numbers studied.
one_liner: Derives exact two-qubit entanglement dynamics with initial reservoir correlations and dynamical decoupling in a dephasing bath.
why_it_matters: Clarifies how pre-existing environment correlations degrade entanglement and how pulse control can extend usable coherence windows.
detailed_summary: The paper treats two qubits coupled to a common bosonic reservoir through a pure dephasing interaction, allowing initial qubit-reservoir correlations formed before state preparation. For an Ohmic spectral density, it obtains exact reduced two-qubit dynamics and evaluates entanglement via Wootters concurrence. Initial correlations accelerate entanglement sudden death relative to factorized assumptions, while symmetric periodic pi-pulse sequences significantly prolong entanglement lifetime.
platform_or_system: two qubits in a common bosonic dephasing reservoir
main_result: The main result is an exact demonstration that initial system-reservoir correlations shorten entanglement lifetime, while dynamical decoupling extends it by nearly a factor of seven in the studied regime.
application_angle: The results inform control protocols for qubit sensors and quantum devices where environmental memory and preparation history affect entanglement preservation.

title: Single-photon addition to multimode quantum fields at telecom wavelengths using lithium niobate and its doped variants
abstract: Multimode spectro-temporal non-Gaussian quantum states of light play a crucial role in continuous-variable quantum information processing. In particular, the non-Gaussian quantum states generated through a single-photon addition (SPA) to multimode quantum fields at telecommunication wavelengths constitute a useful resource for quantum technologies. We present a detailed theoretical analysis and numerical simulations of single-photon addition (SPA) and mode-selective single-photon addition (MSSPA) to a multimode quantum field at telecommunication wavelengths. The analysis is performed for congruently grown lithium niobate (LN), $5\%$ MgO-doped lithium niobate (MgO:LN) and various concentrations of ZnO-doped lithium niobate (ZnO:LN) bulk crystals. We investigate MSSPA using type-II parametric down-conversion (PDC) and SPA using the type-I PDC processes. We further present spectro-temporal mode-selective SPA at the telecom wavelength using $5\%$ MgO:LN for temperatures ranging from $0^\circ C$ to $15^\circ C$. In addition, we perform simulations to investigate SPA based on the noncollinear type-I PDC configuration. These theoretical results identify optimal experimental conditions and phase-matching parameters to achieve SPA and mode-selective SPA for LN-based crystals, providing a potential platform for non-Gaussian quantum state engineering at telecommunication wavelengths, mainly at $1550$ nm.
one_liner: Maps conditions for single-photon addition and mode-selective photon addition in LN-family crystals at 1550 nm.
why_it_matters: Identifies practical phase-matching routes to telecom-band non-Gaussian resources for continuous-variable quantum networks and processors.
detailed_summary: The work provides theoretical analysis and numerical simulations of single-photon addition to multimode quantum fields in congruent LN, MgO:LN, and ZnO:LN bulk crystals. It compares mode-selective SPA via type-II parametric down-conversion with type-I SPA and studies temperature tuning from 0 to 15 degrees C in 5 percent MgO:LN. It also evaluates noncollinear type-I configurations to identify phase-matching conditions for telecom operation around 1550 nm.
platform_or_system: LN-based bulk nonlinear crystals at telecom wavelengths
main_result: The main result is a set of optimized crystal, temperature, and phase-matching conditions for generating single-photon-added multimode non-Gaussian states near 1550 nm.
application_angle: The platform supports experimentally accessible non-Gaussian state engineering for telecom-compatible continuous-variable quantum communication and photonic information processing.

title: Quantum materials QED with van der Waals crystals
abstract: A central goal of the emerging field of materials QED is to harness subwavelength electromagnetic confinement in engineered cavities to tailor light-matter interactions. Here, we demonstrate that van der Waals multilayer cavities composed of stacked graphene and hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) provide unprecedented control over hybridization between their electromagnetic resonances. By magnetically tuning graphene inter-Landau-level transitions (ILTs) into resonance with hBN phonons, we witness broadband, mode-selective strong coupling in the mid-infrared. Our quantum-material QED framework shows that cavity geometry and layer placement jointly control both coupling strength and modal selectivity. For experimentally realistic cavity parameters, the predicted mode splitting exceeds the width of the hBN Reststrahlen band, providing a direct route to the ultrastrong coupling regime. Together, these results establish van der Waals multilayer cavities as a scalable platform for tunable multimode QED and broaden the design space for reconfigurable quantum materials.
one_liner: Demonstrates tunable mid-IR strong coupling between graphene Landau-level transitions and hBN phonons in vdW cavities.
why_it_matters: Shows a scalable design space for reconfigurable multimode quantum-material QED with potential access to ultrastrong coupling.
detailed_summary: The paper studies stacked graphene and hexagonal boron nitride multilayer cavities as a quantum-material QED platform. Magnetic tuning brings graphene inter-Landau-level transitions into resonance with hBN phonons, enabling broadband and mode-selective strong coupling in the mid-infrared. The framework shows that cavity geometry and layer placement control coupling strength and modal selectivity, with predicted splittings exceeding the hBN Reststrahlen-band width for realistic parameters.
platform_or_system: graphene-hBN van der Waals multilayer cavities
main_result: The main result is mode-selective, magnetically tunable strong coupling between graphene electronic transitions and hBN phonon resonances, with a route to ultrastrong coupling.
application_angle: This enables reconfigurable mid-infrared photonic and sensing devices based on compact quantum-material cavities.

title: High-Rate Quantum Codes with Proven Distance and Low-Weight Measurements
abstract: We study a family of quantum subsystem codes defined on rectangular coordinate grids of any dimension, with even side lengths of at least four. The directly measured operators act along coordinate lines. For every member of the family, we derive the number of protected logical qubits and prove its dressed distance without a numerical search. To illustrate the resulting design choices, we impose a budget of at most 10,000 data qubits and determine the complete tradeoff between encoding rate and measurement weight within this family at distances 16, 32, and 64. At distance 16, one code protects 4,096 logical qubits among 10,000 data qubits using weight-ten measurements. At distances 32 and 64, codes with 7,776 and 9,216 data qubits protect 1,024 and 256 logical qubits, respectively, using weight-six measurements. We include and explain Lean code snippets throughout the paper to guide readers through the formal verification of our subsystem-code construction and its dressed and bare distances.
one_liner: Constructs high-rate subsystem quantum codes with proven distances and low-weight line-like measurements on coordinate grids.
why_it_matters: Offers analytically verified code families with favorable rate, distance, and measurement-weight tradeoffs for fault-tolerant hardware design.
detailed_summary: The paper defines subsystem codes on even-sided rectangular coordinate grids in arbitrary dimension, with measured operators supported along coordinate lines. It derives the number of logical qubits and proves dressed distances analytically, supplemented by Lean formal-verification snippets. Under a 10,000-data-qubit budget, the authors map rate versus measurement-weight tradeoffs at distances 16, 32, and 64, including examples encoding thousands of logical qubits with weight-six to weight-ten measurements.
main_result: The main result is a family of high-rate quantum subsystem codes with provable dressed distance and low-weight directly measured operators.
application_angle: These constructions give fault-tolerant quantum-computing architects concrete options for reducing measurement complexity while preserving high encoding rates.

title: Gaussian Fisher Information Is Superadditive
abstract: Quantum Fisher information adds over independent probes, so a single parameter is best measured probe by probe. We show that Gaussian measurements, the linear optics and homodyne detection of optical and microwave experiments, break this rule: two independent modes are better measured together. The uncertainty principle leaves a linear detector half of phase space, and for two modes the choice of half is a resource. Bell homodyne, a balanced beam splitter followed by two homodyne detectors, beats the best separate readout when the modes differ in quadrature width and in how the width responds to the parameter. Heterodyne detection splits a mode on a beam splitter to read both quadratures and pays one unit of vacuum noise for the empty port. Bell homodyne fills that port with the second mode, so the noise turns into signal. We prove that the gain stays below $(\sqrt2-1)^2=17.157\%$ for every parameter carried by widths. For thermal modes at one temperature, the canonical case, a gain was conjectured impossible. We prove that any frequency difference opens a temperature window and that the gain peaks at $12.699\%$ at frequency ratio $3.318$, where Bell homodyne is the optimal Gaussian measurement. Standard hardware reaches the gain: two coupled resonators with two homodyne detectors, or a phase-preserving amplifier whose idler band is fed by the same thermal source.
one_liner: Joint Gaussian readout can extract more Fisher information from independent bosonic modes than separate homodyne or heterodyne measurements.
why_it_matters: It identifies a practical linear-optics advantage for precision thermometry and width-encoded sensing using standard resonators, beam splitters, and homodyne detectors.
detailed_summary: The paper shows that Gaussian measurements violate the usual additivity intuition for independent probes: measuring two modes jointly can outperform the best separate Gaussian readouts. The advantage comes from using the second mode to fill the vacuum port that would otherwise add heterodyne noise. For width-encoded parameters the gain is bounded by 17.157%, and for two thermal modes at one temperature it peaks at 12.699% for a frequency ratio of 3.318.
platform_or_system: two bosonic modes with Gaussian readout
main_result: A Bell-homodyne measurement is proven to provide bounded superadditive Gaussian Fisher information and to be optimal for a thermal-mode case.
application_angle: The scheme maps directly onto coupled optical or microwave resonators and could improve temperature or quadrature-width sensing without exotic hardware.

title: Optimal state detection without likelihood estimation
abstract: We show that adaptive Bayesian estimation in fluorescence state detection reduces to a comparison of elapsed time with two arithmetic time sequences fixed by the bright and dark count rates and confidence parameters $ε_d$ and $ε_b$. No probabilities are computed in real time and the resulting implementation, which we term sequential deadline detection, is provably optimal in mean detection time. The analysis permits closed-form expressions for detection-time distributions, mean detection times, error rates of both channels accounting for miscalibrated rates, decay between the states during detection, and afterpulsing in single photon counting modules. The predictions are validated by Monte Carlo simulation and demonstrated by fluorescence detection with Ba$^+$
one_liner: Fluorescence state detection can be made optimal using simple count-rate deadlines instead of real-time likelihood calculations.
why_it_matters: It turns adaptive Bayesian ion-state readout into a hardware-friendly timing rule with analytic error models and experimental Ba+ validation.
detailed_summary: The work reduces adaptive Bayesian fluorescence detection to comparing elapsed time against two arithmetic deadline sequences set by bright and dark rates and target confidence parameters. This avoids real-time probability evaluation while preserving optimal mean detection time. The authors derive closed-form detection-time and error-rate expressions including rate miscalibration, state decay, and single-photon detector afterpulsing, then validate the predictions with Monte Carlo simulations and Ba+ fluorescence measurements.
main_result: Sequential deadline detection achieves provably optimal mean detection time using only precomputed timing thresholds.
application_angle: The method is well suited to low-latency FPGA or embedded control for trapped-ion experiments and other photon-counting state-readout systems.

title: Random Quantum LDPC Codes Approaching the Gilbert-Varshamov Bound
abstract: We show that for any $R,ε>0$ and any prime $p\geq 2$, there exists an infinite family of $p$-ary quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes, rate $R$, checks of weight $O_ε(1)$, and normalized distance at least $δ_{\mathrm{GV}}(p,R)-ε$. Here, $δ_{\mathrm{GV}}(p,R)$ denotes the quantum Gilbert-Varshamov (GV) bound for $p$-ary stabilizer codes. In fact, we construct an ensemble of such QLDPC codes, such that a random code from this ensemble is close to the GV bound with high probability. Moreover, this ensemble matches the performance of random stabilizer codes on several quantum channels. Specifically, it approaches the quantum capacity of the erasure channel and the hashing bound for memoryless Pauli channels, including the depolarizing channel. A significant challenge in working with QLDPC codes is that they are necessarily \emph{degenerate}, i.e., contain many low-weight stabilizers. A key contribution of our work is a construction of QLDPC codes with quantitative control on their degeneracy. These codes are obtained by combining known constructions of asymptotically good QLDPC codes with the expander-based distance amplification procedure of Alon, Edmonds, and Luby [FOCS'95]. Our random ensemble is constructed by starting with these low-degeneracy QLDPC codes near the quantum Singleton bound and concatenating each coordinate with a random inner code. This can be viewed as a quantum analogue of Thommesen's construction, and as an LDPC version of a result of Ouyang, with an appropriately designed outer code.
one_liner: A random QLDPC construction yields constant-check-weight quantum codes approaching the quantum Gilbert-Varshamov bound.
why_it_matters: Better QLDPC code families are central to reducing overheads in fault-tolerant quantum hardware and quantum memory architectures.
detailed_summary: The paper constructs infinite families of p-ary QLDPC codes with arbitrary positive rate, constant-weight checks, and normalized distance approaching the quantum Gilbert-Varshamov bound. The ensemble also matches random stabilizer-code performance on erasure and memoryless Pauli channels. A key technical ingredient is quantitative control of degeneracy, combining asymptotically good QLDPC outer codes, distance amplification, and random inner-code concatenation.
main_result: Random codes from the proposed QLDPC ensemble approach the quantum GV bound with high probability while retaining constant-weight checks.
application_angle: The construction strengthens the theory base for scalable error-corrected memories and communication codes with practical sparse-check structure.

title: SMP: A General Hyperedge-Based Framework for Circuit-Level Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Hyperedge faults remain a major challenge in circuit-level quantum error correction. Accurately exploiting hyperedge correlations often requires substantial computational resources, which complicates real-time decoding. Matching-based decoders are fast and scalable, but their pairwise graph representation limits the use of higher-order fault information. Here, we introduce Syndrome Motif Projection (SMP), a general framework for incorporating hyperedge information into matching-based decoding. The key idea is that a hyperedge fault produces a characteristic local syndrome motif. Observing such a motif provides evidence for the corresponding fault. SMP extracts this information directly from the measured syndrome with linear-complexity preprocessing while preserving the matching backend. It can therefore serve as a lightweight front end to existing scalable and real-time matching decoders. We demonstrate SMP across surface code memories, color code memories, and logical gate circuits. On Google's Willow experimental surface code data, SMP improves both standard and correlated matching and outperforms the tested belief matching baseline. For color code memories, SMP combined with Chromobius reduces logical failure probabilities by up to 77.8\%. For logical gate circuits, SMP reduces the failure probability of a six-CNOT circuit by 35.5\% relative to logical observable matching while achieving performance comparable to iterative belief matching. These results demonstrate that SMP provides a lightweight and transferable approach to hyperedge decoding, with a clear path toward integration into scalable real-time decoding architectures for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
one_liner: Syndrome Motif Projection injects hyperedge fault information into fast matching decoders through linear-time preprocessing.
why_it_matters: It improves circuit-level decoding on surface codes, color codes, and gate circuits while preserving scalable real-time matching backends.
detailed_summary: SMP identifies local syndrome motifs associated with hyperedge faults and converts that evidence into a form usable by matching-based decoders. The preprocessing is linear complexity and leaves the fast matching backend intact, making it attractive for real-time decoding pipelines. Tests include surface-code memories, color-code memories, logical gate circuits, and Google's Willow experimental surface-code data, where SMP improves over standard and correlated matching baselines.
main_result: SMP improves matching-based decoding, including up to 77.8% lower logical failure probability for color-code memories and 35.5% reduction for a six-CNOT circuit.
application_angle: The framework offers a practical upgrade path for fault-tolerant quantum processors that need better use of correlated circuit faults without abandoning fast decoders.

title: Absence of universal backscattering immunity in reciprocal photonic waveguides
abstract: Suppressing parasitic back-reflection caused by imperfections, such as random defects, material inhomogeneities, localized inclusions, and fabrication-induced geometric deviations, has long been a central objective in optical-waveguide engineering. In this Letter, we theoretically establish that universal immunity to backscattering from arbitrary disorder is fundamentally impossible in reciprocal optical waveguides, irrespective of whether the underlying structure is topologically trivial or nontrivial.We establish this result through two complementary constructions of physically admissible reciprocal perturbations. The first considers weak permittivity perturbations of finite spatial extent within the first Born approximation, whereas the second considers optically small dielectric perturbations of finite contrast. In each construction, an admissible realization exists that produces a nonzero leading-order backward-scattering amplitude. We trace the fundamental origin of this limitation to the absence in photons of the intrinsic spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ and fermionic time-reversal structure underlying Kramers protection in electronic systems. Consequently, any mechanism that enforces photonic backscattering suppression throughout a prescribed class of disorder must instead be engineered into the underlying electromagnetic structure and its constitutive response, which can itself be modified by generic reciprocal perturbations. Numerical examples in representative reciprocal topological waveguides further illustrate these limitations for random defects and sharp bends. We further identify several constructive strategies for suppressing back-reflection within certain prescribed classes of disorder.
one_liner: Reciprocal photonic waveguides cannot be universally immune to backscattering from arbitrary admissible disorder.
why_it_matters: It clarifies a fundamental limit for topological and reciprocal waveguide design, preventing overclaims of disorder-proof photonic transport.
detailed_summary: The paper proves that arbitrary reciprocal disorder can always be chosen to create nonzero leading-order backward scattering in optical waveguides. The result is shown using finite weak permittivity perturbations and finite-contrast optically small dielectric perturbations. The limitation is traced to the absence of fermionic Kramers protection for photons, with numerical examples illustrating failures in reciprocal topological waveguides under defects and bends.
main_result: Universal backscattering immunity is shown to be impossible for reciprocal photonic waveguides, even when the nominal structure is topological.
application_angle: The result helps designers target realistic disorder classes and engineered suppression mechanisms rather than assuming blanket topological protection.

title: Quantum Error-Corrected Memories Keep Proper Time
abstract: What does quantum error correction do to relativistic proper time? We show that when two error-corrected quantum memories follow distinct worldlines and are controlled by local references, their local correction histories factor exactly from the proper-time difference between them. Error correction therefore does not erase time dilation: when the memories are compared, the accumulated difference appears as a relational phase rotation. During locally referenced operation this rotation is invisible to every local error syndrome; at discrete phases admitted by a code, the final relational evolution instead returns exactly as a deterministic logical gate, including an $S$-type Clifford gate at a $π/2$ excursion. These results connect fault-tolerant quantum information with relativistic clocks and establish protected quantum memories as a platform for preserving proper-time information and for long-coherence tests of quantum evolution involving relativistic proper time.
one_liner: Error-corrected quantum memories retain relativistic proper-time differences as protected relational logical phases.
why_it_matters: It links fault-tolerant memories with relativistic clock physics and suggests long-coherence tests of proper-time-dependent quantum evolution.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes two locally controlled error-corrected memories following different worldlines and shows that local correction histories factor from their proper-time difference. Time dilation is therefore not erased by QEC; it appears as a relational phase when the memories are compared. At code-admitted discrete phases, the relational evolution can return as a deterministic logical gate, including an S-type Clifford gate at a pi/2 excursion.
main_result: Quantum error correction preserves proper-time information as a relational logical phase rather than removing it through local correction.
application_angle: Protected memories could serve as long-coherence platforms for relativistic quantum sensing, clock comparison, and tests of proper-time effects in quantum hardware.

title: From Heat to Homology: Spectral Gap Transfer for Exact Quantum Gibbs Sampling at All Temperatures
abstract: Preparing Gibbs states through dissipative dynamics requires controlling convergence for the chosen Hamiltonian $H$ and coupling operators. However, efficient implementation requires convergence guarantees from the spectral gap of the generator of the dynamics, which remains a crucial challenge. Recent results address the challenge by restricting the dynamics with structural assumptions about the Hamiltonian and its interactions. For the Chen-Kastoryano-Gilyen (CKG) construction and arbitrary finite-dimensional Hamiltonians, we prove an explicit comparison that converts a spectral gap estimate for the infinite-temperature generator into a lower bound on the spectral gap of the CKG quantum Gibbs sampler at every finite positive inverse temperature $β$. It allows a single spectral gap estimate at infinite temperature to certify convergence across Hamiltonians and temperatures. Such an estimate is often known from a classical spectral gap estimate, such as the classical random walk spectral gap. For Hodge Laplacians of simplicial complexes as Hamiltonians, we construct coupling operators whose generator at infinite temperature has the same spectral gap as a classical simplicial down-up walk. A positive spectral gap of the walk and bounded spectral width $W=λ_{\max}(H)-λ_{\min}(H)$ give a generator spectral gap independent of the number of simplices at every fixed temperature. We then establish conditions under which the sampler approximately prepares zero-energy (harmonic) states in polynomial evolution time. This provides a conditional convergence guarantee for the state preparation in the thermal approach to quantum topological data analysis.
one_liner: Proves spectral-gap transfer bounds for CKG quantum Gibbs samplers, enabling certified convergence from infinite to finite temperature.
why_it_matters: Gives a route to provable Gibbs-state preparation for arbitrary finite-dimensional Hamiltonians and topological-data-analysis Hamiltonians.
detailed_summary: The paper proves an explicit comparison theorem that lower-bounds the finite-temperature CKG quantum Gibbs sampler gap using the infinite-temperature generator gap. For Hodge Laplacians on simplicial complexes, it constructs couplings whose infinite-temperature gap matches a classical simplicial down-up walk. Under bounded spectral width and positive walk gap, the sampler has system-size-independent gap at fixed temperature and can approximately prepare harmonic zero-energy states in polynomial time.
main_result: A single infinite-temperature gap estimate can certify finite-temperature convergence for CKG Gibbs sampling, including Hodge-Laplacian instances.
application_angle: This supports more certifiable quantum algorithms for thermal state preparation and quantum topological data analysis.

title: Quasiparticle quantum simulation of materials with the Bethe-Salpeter equation
abstract: The first-principles quantum simulation of the full electronic Hamiltonian of a material model of realistic size appears daunting even in a future era of fully fault-tolerant quantum computers. In contrast, classical simulations of material excited states rely on heuristic quasiparticle frameworks, such as the GW approximation and Bethe-Salpeter equation, where only a few quasiparticles are explicitly considered. Here we give a detailed description of quasiparticle quantum simulation for multi-excitonic states within the BSE. We develop an explicit first-quantized, orbital-based block encoding of the multi-exciton BSE Hamiltonian for qubitization, and reduce its cost using integral factorization and crystal symmetries. For a materials model of size $N$, and a fixed number of quasiparticles, the resulting algorithms require $\widetilde{O}(N)$ Toffoli gates and $O(\log N)$ logical qubits, or, using space-time tradeoffs, $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{N})$ Toffoli gates and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{N})$ logical qubits, achieving up to a sixth power reduction in Toffoli count, or up to exponential reduction in qubit count, versus standard full Hamiltonian simulation techniques that have been explored in materials simulation. Resource estimates for the classically challenging problem of triexcitonic eigenvalue estimation across a range of semiconductor models of a realistic physical size of $O(10^3)$ atoms, show that our Toffoli-optimized implementation reduces the Toffoli count by $10^6-10^7$ relative to full Hamiltonian simulation estimates, while a qubit-optimized implementation requires only a few hundred logical qubits. More broadly, these results show that classical heuristic frameworks will be essential in the design of future fault-tolerant quantum algorithms for materials.
one_liner: Develops first-quantized qubitization algorithms for multi-exciton Bethe-Salpeter Hamiltonians with large resource savings.
why_it_matters: Shows how quasiparticle models can make fault-tolerant quantum simulation of realistic semiconductor excitations far cheaper.
detailed_summary: The work formulates a first-quantized, orbital-based block encoding for multi-exciton BSE Hamiltonians and optimizes it with integral factorization and crystal symmetries. For fixed quasiparticle number, costs scale as roughly linear Toffoli count with logarithmic logical qubits, or with a space-time tradeoff as square-root scaling in both. Resource estimates for triexcitonic eigenvalue estimation in O(10^3)-atom semiconductor models show 10^6-10^7 Toffoli-count reductions versus full electronic-Hamiltonian simulation.
main_result: The algorithm estimates multi-excitonic BSE spectra with dramatically reduced Toffoli and logical-qubit resources.
application_angle: It makes optoelectronic materials, exciton physics, and semiconductor excited-state modeling more plausible targets for future fault-tolerant devices.

title: Interaction-induced period shift of the Kohn oscillation in a parity-time-symmetric harmonic trap
abstract: The center of mass of a Bose--Einstein condensate in a harmonic trap oscillates at the trap frequency independently of the interactions. Without interactions a parity-time-symmetric gain-loss gradient leaves this frequency unchanged, and a cloud of the ground-state width is translated rigidly while the atom number is periodically modulated. With interactions the protection is lost, because the gain and the loss change the number of atoms; the modulated atom number drives the width of the cloud, and the width acts back on the center of mass. At small gain the period grows quadratically with the gain strength, with a coefficient that in the Thomas--Fermi regime is set by the size of the cloud alone. The family of periodic orbits continued from the Kohn oscillation can be followed up to a critical gain, where it comes into resonance with highly excited states of the trap, and over the computed families this critical gain decreases with the amplitude of the oscillation and with the size of the cloud. A five-variable moment model reproduces the period and the width of the cloud along the orbits nearly up to the critical gain.
one_liner: Analyzes how interactions shift Kohn-oscillation periods in a gain-loss PT-symmetric Bose-Einstein-condensate trap.
why_it_matters: Identifies measurable interaction-driven dynamics in non-Hermitian atom-optics platforms and provides a compact predictive moment model.
detailed_summary: The study considers a Bose-Einstein condensate in a harmonic trap with a parity-time-symmetric gain-loss gradient. Without interactions, the center-of-mass oscillation remains protected, but interactions couple atom-number modulation to cloud width and then back to the center of mass. The period grows quadratically with gain at small gain, and a five-variable moment model reproduces the orbit period and width nearly up to a critical gain where resonances appear.
main_result: Interactions break Kohn-period protection and produce a gain-dependent period shift captured by a reduced moment model.
application_angle: The effect offers a diagnostic handle for engineered non-Hermitian matter-wave systems and precision control of gain-loss condensate dynamics.

title: Metasurface-on-Lithium-Niobate Architecture for Spin-decoupled Second Harmonic Wavefront Shaping
abstract: Nonlinear metasurfaces (NMSs) enable simultaneous generation and manipulation of harmonic light with ultrathin nanophotonic platforms. However, conventional NMSs typically adopt a monolithic single-layer configuration in which frequency conversion, polarization selection and wavefront engineering are intertwined to simultaneously occur within the same nonlinear meta-atoms, making these functionalities intrinsically interdependent and imposing constraints on material choice, structural symmetry, and the available geometric parameter space. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a metasurface-on-lithium-niobate architecture that physically separates harmonic light generation and wavefront manipulation. In this platform, a z-cut thin-film LN layer serves as a spin-selective second-harmonic source through its intrinsic bulk second-order nonlinearity, while an overlaid dielectric metasurface subsequently and independently molds wavefronts of generated harmonic fields. The two-step process, by virtue of harmonic generation being decoupled from wavefront shaping, removes symmetry constraints associated with conventional nonlinear meta-atoms and enables the direct transfer of well-established linear metasurface design strategies to harmonic wavefront engineering. As proof-of-concept demonstrations, we realize spin-decoupled second-harmonic beam steering and spin-multiplexed holography, achieving high-contrast routing of harmonic signals with orthogonal spin states into distinct diffraction channels and high-fidelity reconstruction of independent holographic images. By redirecting the harmonic wavefront control from the meta-atom engineering to the modular system-level design, our approach establishes a versatile route toward integrated nonlinear meta-optics and provides a scalable platform for advanced optical functionalities.
one_liner: Demonstrates a metasurface-on-lithium-niobate platform that decouples SHG generation from spin-dependent wavefront shaping.
why_it_matters: Modularly separates nonlinear conversion and optical routing, expanding design freedom for integrated nonlinear meta-optics.
detailed_summary: The authors place a dielectric metasurface over z-cut thin-film lithium niobate so the LN layer generates spin-selective second-harmonic light while the metasurface independently shapes the harmonic wavefront. This avoids the symmetry and parameter constraints of monolithic nonlinear meta-atoms. Experiments demonstrate spin-decoupled second-harmonic beam steering and spin-multiplexed holography with distinct routing channels and independent image reconstruction.
main_result: The platform experimentally realizes independent spin-controlled second-harmonic beam steering and holographic wavefront control.
application_angle: It provides a scalable architecture for integrated nonlinear photonic routing, multiplexing, holography, and compact frequency-converting optical components.

title: Certification of high-dimensional entanglement in continuous-variable systems
abstract: The dimensionality of entanglement in high-dimensional quantum systems is quantified by the Schmidt number, whose large value signals potential advantages for quantum communication and quantum computation. A commonly used approach to practical Schmidt-number detection in finite-dimensional systems is based on the estimation of fidelities to pure states with large entanglement dimensionality or lower bounds to these fidelities. However, for mode-entangled continuous-variable systems, the corresponding measurements are typically difficult to realize. Here, we introduce and assess fidelity bounds for Schmidt-number detection based on practically more accessible measurements of the first and second statistical moments of arbitrary continuous-variable quantum states. We provide analytical formulas that allow evaluating these bounds and test them for families of Gaussian and non-Gaussian states, including two-mode squeezed thermal states and photon-added displaced two-mode squeezed vacuum states. We compare our bounds to other methods for the certification of high-dimensional entanglement based on the same measurements.
one_liner: Introduces practical Schmidt-number certification bounds for continuous-variable entanglement using first and second moments.
why_it_matters: Makes high-dimensional entanglement certification more accessible for CV quantum communication experiments.
detailed_summary: The paper develops fidelity bounds for detecting Schmidt number in mode-entangled continuous-variable states using experimentally accessible first- and second-moment measurements. It gives analytical formulas and evaluates them on Gaussian and non-Gaussian families, including two-mode squeezed thermal states and photon-added displaced two-mode squeezed vacuum states. The method is compared against other certification approaches using the same measurement data.
main_result: First- and second-moment data can lower-bound fidelities strongly enough to certify high-dimensional CV entanglement in selected state families.
application_angle: The approach reduces measurement overhead for validating entanglement dimensionality in CV quantum networks and communication protocols.

title: Self-organized Layered Structures of Nitrogen-Vacancy Centers with Preferential Orientation in Heteroepitaxial Diamond Films
abstract: Here, we report the fabrication and characterization of single crystal diamond films on a two-inch wafer-scale containing three-dimensional layered structures of negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy color centers (NV$^{-}$). The (100)-oriented layered diamond films were grown by chemical vapor deposition (CVD) to create spatially separated regions of enhanced emission associated with NV$^{-}$ centers. Such localized emission enhancement as well as 2D and 3D arrays of spins could enable close-packed architectures for emerging quantum devices, such as data processors, memory cells, and magnetic sensors. A cyclic sequence of CVD growth and oxygen-plasma etching is employed, resulting in the in-situ formation of layered inverted pyramidal structures with flat $\{$111$\}$ sidewalls. These pits are subsequently overgrown by nitrogen-doped diamond to achieve NV$^{-}$-rich facets with a uniform N-V bond arrangement and improved nitrogen incorporation efficiency.
one_liner: Reports wafer-scale heteroepitaxial diamond films with self-organized layered NV-center structures and preferential orientation.
why_it_matters: Offers a materials route to dense, spatially organized NV spin arrays for scalable quantum sensing and device integration.
detailed_summary: The authors fabricate single-crystal diamond films on two-inch wafers containing three-dimensional layered structures enriched in negatively charged NV centers. A cyclic CVD growth and oxygen-plasma etching process forms inverted pyramidal features with flat {111} sidewalls, which are then overgrown with nitrogen-doped diamond. The resulting NV-rich facets show localized emission enhancement, preferential N-V bond arrangement, and improved nitrogen incorporation efficiency.
main_result: The process creates layered, preferentially oriented NV-rich diamond structures across a two-inch heteroepitaxial wafer.
application_angle: Such ordered NV ensembles are relevant for close-packed magnetic sensors, spin memories, and integrated diamond quantum-device architectures.

title: Landscape-Dependent Performance of Photonic Quantum Solvers in QUBO Feature Selection for Financial Risk Detection
abstract: Feature selection for imbalanced classification tasks such as credit card fraud and consumer default detection requires balancing predictive relevance, inter-feature redundancy, and computational feasibility. We benchmark three computing paradigms, classical branch-and-bound optimization (Gurobi), photonic entropy computing (QCI Dirac-3), and simulated photonic boson sampling (Piquasso), across thirteen feature-selection methods on two datasets: ULB Credit Card Fraud (30 features) and AmEx consumer default (159 features). Each method is routed to the solver matched to its mathematical structure. On ULB, Dirac-3 MI-Spearman matches the all-features model using 13 of 30 features (mean F1 0.873 +/- 0.023 over five runs, best run 0.896), and Piquasso is the best method at k=5. On AmEx, performance rises steadily with the feature budget and every paradigm approaches F1 = 0.80 only near the full feature set. Most differences between Gurobi and Dirac-3 on identical methods fall within run-to-run variation; the large gaps occur where the certified optimum generalizes poorly, most sharply for distance correlation on AmEx at k=25 (Gurobi F1 = 0.422 vs. a Dirac-3 mean of 0.746). At matched budgets, F1 varies about ten times more across methods on ULB than on AmEx, which we trace to how concentrated the predictive signal is in each feature space.
one_liner: Benchmarks photonic and classical QUBO solvers for feature selection in fraud and default-risk detection tasks.
why_it_matters: It tests near-term photonic optimization hardware on realistic financial ML workloads where solver landscape and generalization both matter.
detailed_summary: The paper compares Gurobi, QCI Dirac-3 photonic entropy computing, and simulated photonic boson sampling on QUBO-style feature selection for ULB fraud and AmEx default datasets. Dirac-3 MI-Spearman matches the all-feature ULB model with 13 of 30 features, while Piquasso performs best at k=5. On AmEx, all paradigms only approach F1 near the full feature set, emphasizing that landscape and feature-signal concentration dominate solver gains.
main_result: Photonic solvers achieved competitive feature-selection performance, including ULB F1 near the all-feature baseline using fewer than half the features.
application_angle: The work probes whether photonic optimization hardware can become useful for practical high-dimensional risk-screening pipelines.

title: Self-testing ideal quantum measurements
abstract: A fundamental prediction of quantum mechanics is that observables can be measured through ideal measurements, that is, measurements that give the same outcome when repeated and do not disturb any observable that is jointly measurable. In terms of quantum instruments, such an ideal measurement is described by projective effects together with the associated Luders state-update rule. Here, we show that quantum mechanics allows for self-testing any ideal measurement. Using solely the output statistics of bipartite Bell tests in which a non-demolition measurement is sometimes added, it is possible to certify in a device-independent manner whether the added measurement is ideal.
one_liner: Shows how bipartite Bell-test statistics can device-independently certify ideal quantum measurements.
why_it_matters: Self-testing ideal measurements strengthens trust in black-box quantum devices without assuming their internal implementation.
detailed_summary: The work proves that any ideal measurement, with projective effects and the corresponding Luders state update, can be self-tested from observed statistics. The protocol uses bipartite Bell tests in which a non-demolition measurement is inserted in some rounds. Certification relies only on input-output correlations, making it device-independent rather than hardware-model dependent.
main_result: The paper establishes a method to certify whether an added non-demolition measurement is ideal using only Bell-test output statistics.
application_angle: This is relevant for certifying measurement quality in untrusted quantum communication, networking, and photonic-device scenarios.

title: Emergent Dissipation from Fluctuating Quantum-Network Topology
abstract: We investigate how dissipation can emerge in a quantum network from temporal fluctuations of the interaction topology. For a network whose graph is redrawn at short time intervals, the averaged dynamics yields a Markovian master equation: the mean network fixes the coherent part and the covariance fixes the dissipative structure. The covariance eigenvalues set the noise strengths, while its eigenvectors determine the collective operators on which those strengths act. Two ensembles with identical mean adjacency and covariance spectra but different eigenvectors produce distinct dynamics despite identical purity. A physically realizable model yields an analytically predicted dissipative gap, giving quasi-protected dynamics. These results establish fluctuating connectivity as a resource for engineering quantum dissipation and protection.
one_liner: Derives Markovian dissipation from rapidly fluctuating quantum-network topology.
why_it_matters: It turns network connectivity noise into a tunable resource for engineered dissipation and quasi-protected quantum dynamics.
detailed_summary: The paper studies quantum networks whose interaction graph is redrawn over short time intervals and shows that the averaged dynamics becomes a Markovian master equation. The mean adjacency controls coherent evolution, while graph covariance sets dissipative strengths and collective jump operators. Different covariance eigenvectors can yield distinct dynamics even when spectra and purity are identical, and a realizable model produces an analytic dissipative gap.
main_result: Temporal topology fluctuations generate controllable coherent and dissipative terms, including analytically predicted quasi-protected dynamics.
application_angle: The framework could guide dissipation engineering for quantum communication networks and networked quantum processors.

title: Quantum code parameters, checkable by a certificate of provable size
abstract: A code is described by three numbers: its physical qubits, its logical qubits, and the smallest error it cannot detect, counted in qubits. The first two are linear algebra. The third, the distance, is an optimum over an exponentially large set, read off a solver whose answer carries no certificate. Whether a code's parameters can be checked uniformly across codes, with a certificate of proved size, is open. Here we show that they can, by moving the unit of work from the code to a \emph{certificate}, a short object, either a list, a pairing or a symbolic instance, whose correctness the kernel of the \Lean\ proof assistant decides by computation. The kernel is the small core that checks each step. The certificate's size is itself a theorem: its enumeration form lists the vectors of weight below the distance $d$, $\sum_{j<d}\binom{n}{j}$ of them, a polynomial in the code's length $n$ at fixed distance $d$. No bound uniform over codes in both $n$ and $d$ is smaller. For product families the certificate is smaller still, the bound being proved once, symbolically. Deciding that a vector lies outside the row space of the check matrix, the set of sums of its rows, becomes one matrix-vector product and one inner product. On an eighteen-qubit toric code, a surface code closed into a torus, the whole-file check of that decision falls from 42\,s to 9\,s. Eleven code families and thirty-nine parameter sets follow, the widest at 1872 qubits. Nothing beyond the three standard axioms of \Lean's logic is trusted, though the generator that writes a code's checks stops at twenty qubits, and the lower bound for the 144-qubit code is imported rather than proved here. A distance becomes checkable rather than believed, and the same move applies wherever else a computation ends in a solver.
one_liner: Uses Lean-checkable certificates to verify quantum code distances and parameters at provable certificate sizes.
why_it_matters: It makes error-correcting-code claims independently checkable instead of relying on opaque solver outputs.
detailed_summary: The paper reformulates quantum-code distance verification around compact certificates whose correctness is checked by the Lean proof-assistant kernel. Enumeration certificates list all vectors below distance d, with polynomial size in n at fixed d, while product families can use smaller symbolic certificates. The approach is demonstrated across eleven code families and thirty-nine parameter sets, including systems up to 1872 qubits.
main_result: Quantum code parameters, including distance claims, are made checkable by Lean certificates with proved size bounds.
application_angle: Reliable code-parameter verification supports hardware roadmaps where fault-tolerance thresholds depend on trusted error-correction data.

title: Covertness as a resource constraint in quantum target sensing
abstract: Quantum covert target sensing aims to detect low-reflectivity targets embedded in the thermal environment while avoiding discovery by an adversary. This covertness requirement constrains the admissible probe energy, thereby imposing a trade-off between covertness and sensing performance. However, how this resource constraint determines the ultimate estimation precision of the target parameter remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we establish a unified framework connecting covert target discrimination with quantum-enhanced parameter estimation. We first present perturbative $ε$-covertness-induced bounds on the probe energy, which yield an admissible energy window narrowing as $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{ε/M})$. Moreover, we introduce the covertness-constrained quantum Fisher information (CCQFI) to quantify the ultimate precision of target-reflectivity estimation and assess its attainability with specific measurements. For Gaussian-distributed coherent-state (GCS) and two-mode squeezed vacuum (TMSV) probes, their CCQFIs scale as $\mathcal{O}(ε)$ and $\mathcal{O}(M)+\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{εM})+\mathcal{O}(ε)$, respectively. In particular, in the strong covertness regime $ε\to0$, the GCS CCQFI vanishes, whereas the TMSV retains a finite $\mathcal{O}(M)$ contribution exhibiting a pronounced metrological advantage. Besides, photon counting saturates the GCS CCQFI, whereas homodyne detection achieves a higher attainability for the TMSV probe. Our work identifies covertness as a quantitative resource constraint governing the metrological limits of quantum target sensing.
one_liner: Quantifies how covert-operation constraints bound quantum target-sensing precision.
why_it_matters: It connects stealth requirements to quantum Fisher information, clarifying when quantum probes retain sensing advantage under low detectability.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a framework linking covert target discrimination to covertness-constrained quantum Fisher information for reflectivity estimation. It derives epsilon-covertness energy bounds whose admissible window narrows as O(sqrt(epsilon/M)). Gaussian-distributed coherent probes lose CCQFI in the strong-covertness limit, whereas TMSV probes retain a finite O(M) term, with photon counting optimal for GCS and homodyne more attainable for TMSV.
main_result: Two-mode squeezed vacuum probes retain a finite metrological advantage under strong covertness constraints where coherent-state probes do not.
application_angle: The results inform low-probability-of-detection quantum sensing and lidar designs in thermal backgrounds.

title: Two-body control of noiseless subsystems with mixed $SU(3)$ representations lifts teleportation above the classical fidelity limit
abstract: Collective noise can leave degrees of freedom unaffected, allowing them to store quantum information. Processing this information also requires physically available logical gates. We consider $r$ fundamental qutrits transforming under $U\in SU(3)$ and $s$ dual qutrits transforming under its complex conjugate $\overline U$, with collective action $R_{r,s}(U)=U^{\otimes r}\otimes\overline U^{\otimes s}$. Using the image of the walled Brauer algebra and Lie-algebra arguments, we show that adjacent exchanges within each qutrit type and one singlet-projector interaction between the two types generate any independently chosen family of special unitary gates on the noiseless subsystems by a finite pulse sequence, for every $r,s\geq1$. This establishes semi-universality of this system. We illustrate the result with a numerically optimised sequence of 24 pulses for three fundamental qutrits and one dual qutrit. We then use the encoding and available logical corrections for qutrit teleportation under correlated Weyl noise.
